guides.title: How to Prepare for NISM Series V-A in 15 Days
guides.description: A practical 15-day plan to prepare for NISM Series V-A: daily chapter schedule, approximate weightage, revision days and timed mock tests before exam day.
guides.primary: how to prepare for nism series v-a
secondary: nism mutual fund distributor exam preparation
how to pass nism series v-a
guides.intro: If you are wondering how to prepare for NISM Series V-A without taking weeks off work, a focused 15-day plan is usually enough for most working professionals. The Mutual Fund Distributors exam is not mathematically heavy, but it is detail-heavy: scheme categories, regulatory limits, loads, taxation rules and investor service timelines all appear as tricky one-liners. This guide gives you a day-by-day schedule, an approximate sense of which chapters carry more weight, a revision routine and a mock-test schedule, so that you walk into the test centre knowing exactly where you stand.

sections.heading: Understand the exam pattern first
paragraphs: Before you open the workbook, be clear about what you are preparing for. The indicative pattern is 100 questions carrying 100 marks, to be answered in 120 minutes, with a passing score of 50 percent. There is negative marking of 0.25 marks for each wrong answer. Treat these numbers as indicative — confirm in the latest official notification on nism.ac.in before you book your slot, because NISM revises workbooks and patterns from time to time.

Two things follow from this pattern. First, 120 minutes for 100 questions is generous, so speed is rarely the problem; accuracy is. Second, negative marking means guessing blindly on ten questions can cost you more than two and a half marks, which matters when the pass line is 50. Your preparation should therefore aim at confident recall of facts rather than vague familiarity.

sections.heading: Chapter weightage, approximately
paragraphs: NISM does not publish an official chapter-wise mark split, so the guidance below is approximate and based on the syllabus and the relative length of each workbook chapter. Use it to prioritise, not to skip anything.
bullets: Higher weight (spend the most time): Concept and Role of a Mutual Fund; Legal and Regulatory Framework; Scheme Related Information; NAV, TER and Pricing of Units; Mutual Fund Scheme Selection.
Medium weight: Investment Landscape; Legal Structure of Mutual Funds; Taxation; Investor Services; Risk, Return and Performance of Funds.
Lower but scoring: Fund Distribution and Channel Management; Mutual Fund Scheme Performance (largely definitions and benchmark concepts).
Numerical questions usually come from NAV, TER, loads, returns (absolute, CAGR, SIP returns) and tax calculations — expect a handful, not dozens.

sections.heading: The 15-day study plan
paragraphs: Plan for roughly two hours on weekdays and three to four hours on weekends. Read the workbook chapter first, make one page of notes, and then attempt chapter-wise practice questions the same day while the material is fresh.
bullets: Day 1: Investment Landscape — savings vs investment, asset classes, risk profiling basics, life-cycle needs.
Day 2: Concept and Role of a Mutual Fund — advantages, limitations, scheme classification as per SEBI categorisation.
Day 3: Legal Structure of Mutual Funds — sponsor, trustees, AMC, custodian, RTA; who appoints whom and who reports to whom.
Day 4: Legal and Regulatory Framework — SEBI and AMFI roles, code of conduct, due diligence, investor rights.
Day 5: Scheme Related Information — SID, SAI, KIM, and what each document must contain; first chapter-wise practice set.
Day 6: Fund Distribution and Channel Management — distributor types, ARN, EUIN, commissions and empanelment.
Day 7: NAV, TER and Pricing of Units — practise every formula until you can do it on rough paper without notes.
Day 8: Taxation — capital gains on equity and debt-oriented funds, dividend (IDCW) taxation, STT. Note that tax rules change through Finance Acts, so read the current workbook edition.
Day 9: Investor Services — NFO process, KYC, transaction timelines, SIP/SWP/STP, nomination and transmission.
Day 10: Risk, Return and Performance of Funds — standard deviation, beta, Sharpe ratio, risk-o-meter.
Day 11: Mutual Fund Scheme Performance and Scheme Selection — benchmarks, tracking error, matching schemes to investor profiles.
Day 12: First full-length timed mock test, followed by two hours of reviewing every wrong and every guessed answer.
Day 13: Revise the three weakest chapters from the mock; second full-length mock in the evening.
Day 14: Formula sheet and regulatory numbers revision; third mock test.
Day 15: Light revision of your one-page notes only, sleep early, and check your admit details and centre location.

sections.heading: How to revise so the facts stay
paragraphs: V-A rewards precise recall. Many wrong answers come from confusing two similar-sounding entities — for example, the trustee and the AMC, or the SID and the SAI. On every revision day, test yourself by writing answers from memory before looking at notes.

Keep a running 'error log' in a notebook: the question topic, what you answered, the correct answer and the one-line reason. By Day 13 this log is your most valuable revision material because it reflects your personal blind spots, not a generic summary.
bullets: Make a single sheet of all numerical limits and timelines mentioned in the workbook, and revise it daily from Day 8.
Draw the mutual fund structure as a diagram once; it fixes the roles of sponsor, trustee, AMC, custodian and RTA in memory.
Re-solve every NAV and TER question you got wrong rather than just reading the explanation.
Read regulatory chapters twice — once for understanding, once for the exact wording.

sections.heading: Mock-test schedule and how to use it
paragraphs: Take at least three full-length timed mock tests in the last four days. Sit them in one stretch, without notes and with a timer set to 120 minutes, so the conditions resemble the real test. After each attempt, spend as long reviewing the explanations as you spent writing the test; the review is where most of the learning happens.

Track three numbers per mock: your score, the number of questions you skipped, and your accuracy on attempted questions. If accuracy on attempted questions is below about 75 percent, slow down and skip more; if it is above 90 percent and you are skipping a lot, you are being too cautious.

sections.heading: Common mistakes to avoid
paragraphs: The commonest mistake is reading the workbook cover to cover once and assuming that is enough. Passive reading creates familiarity, and familiarity feels like knowledge until you face four similar options. The second mistake is ignoring the taxation and investor services chapters because they look dry; they are full of direct, factual questions.
Finally, do not rely on old notes or third-party summaries for numbers. Limits, tax rates and timelines are revised, and the current workbook on nism.ac.in is the reference the exam follows.

sections.heading: What to do on exam day
paragraphs: Do a first pass answering everything you are sure of, marking the rest for review. In the second pass, attempt marked questions only where you can eliminate at least two options. With negative marking at 0.25, an educated guess between two options is reasonable; a blind guess between four is not. Leave ten minutes at the end to check that you have not left questions you meant to answer unmarked.

faqs: Is 15 days enough to prepare for NISM Series V-A?

For most graduates who can study two to three hours a day, 15 days is a realistic window. Freshers with no exposure to financial markets may want 20 to 25 days, giving extra time to Taxation, NAV calculations and the regulatory chapters, and to take more full-length practice tests before booking.
Which chapters are most important for NISM V-A?

Based on the syllabus, the regulatory framework, scheme related information, NAV and TER, and scheme selection chapters tend to carry the most questions. NISM does not publish an official split, so read every chapter and use weightage only to decide where to spend extra revision time.
How many mock tests should I take before the NISM V-A exam?

Aim for at least three full-length timed attempts in the final week, plus chapter-wise practice after each topic. The number matters less than the review: go through every wrong and guessed answer, note the reason, and revise that concept before your next attempt.

guides.title: NISM V-A vs V-B: Which Mutual Fund Exam Do You Need?
guides.description: NISM V-A vs V-B explained: who each mutual fund certification is for, how the syllabus and pattern differ, and how to decide which exam to take first.
secondary: difference between nism v-a and v-b
which nism exam for mutual fund distributor
mutual fund foundation vs mutual fund distributors exam
guides.intro: The NISM V-A vs V-B question comes up the moment someone decides to sell mutual funds. Both are mutual fund certifications from NISM, both appear on the same registration pages, and both lead into the distribution business — yet they serve different people. Series V-A (Mutual Fund Distributors) is the full certification for distributors who want to sell the complete range of schemes. Series V-B (Mutual Fund Foundation) is a shorter, foundation-level exam aimed at a new cadre of distributors who sell only a limited set of simpler schemes. This guide compares the two and helps you pick the right one.

sections.heading: The short answer
paragraphs: If you intend to build a mutual fund distribution practice, work as a relationship manager in a bank or wealth firm, or advise clients across equity, hybrid and debt schemes, you need NISM Series V-A. It is the standard certification behind an AMFI Registration Number (ARN) for regular distributors.

Series V-B suits people who will distribute only the restricted basket of simple products permitted for the new-cadre category, or who want a gentle, entry-level introduction to mutual funds before attempting V-A. The exact list of eligible persons and permitted schemes is set by SEBI and AMFI, so check the current rules on amfiindia.com and the exam details on nism.ac.in before deciding.

sections.heading: Pattern comparison at a glance
paragraphs: The indicative patterns below come from the current exam structure as we understand it. They are indicative — confirm in the latest official notification on nism.ac.in, since NISM updates patterns and workbooks.
bullets: V-A: 100 questions, 100 marks, 120 minutes, pass mark 50 percent, negative marking of 0.25 per wrong answer.
V-B: 50 questions, 50 marks, 60 minutes, pass mark 50 percent, no negative marking.
V-A is roughly twice the length and penalises wrong answers, so guessing strategy matters more.
V-B's shorter paper and absence of negative marking make it noticeably less stressful for first-time candidates.

sections.heading: How the syllabus differs
paragraphs: V-B covers the basics: what a mutual fund is, simple product types, how investors transact, essential investor services and the regulatory environment at an introductory level. It is designed so that someone with no finance background can follow it.

V-A goes much deeper. Its workbook spans the investment landscape, the legal structure of mutual funds (sponsor, trustee, AMC, custodian, RTA), the SEBI and AMFI regulatory framework, scheme documents such as the SID, SAI and KIM, distribution and channel management, NAV, TER and pricing of units, taxation of mutual fund investments, investor services, risk and return measures, scheme performance evaluation and scheme selection for different investor profiles.

The biggest jumps in difficulty are in three places: numerical questions on NAV, loads and returns; taxation of equity-oriented and other schemes; and scheme selection questions that describe an investor and ask which category fits. None of these is extremely hard, but they need practice rather than one reading.

sections.heading: Who should take V-A
paragraphs: Choose V-A if any of the following describes you. It is the more widely recognised certification and keeps your options open as your business grows.
bullets: You want to sell equity, hybrid, debt and solution-oriented schemes to retail and HNI clients.
You are joining a bank branch, broking firm or wealth management team in a sales or relationship role involving mutual funds.
You plan to move later towards NISM Series X-A and X-B (investment adviser) or XXI-A (PMS distributors), where V-A level knowledge is a useful base.
Your employer or the AMCs you want to empanel with ask specifically for the V-A certificate.

sections.heading: Who should take V-B
paragraphs: V-B makes sense for candidates who fall within the new-cadre distributor category defined by the regulators and will work only with the limited set of simple schemes that category allows. It also works as a confidence-building first step for someone completely new to finance who wants to understand the basics before tackling V-A.

Keep in mind that V-B does not replace V-A for regular distribution. If there is a reasonable chance you will want to sell the full product range within a year or two, it is usually more efficient to prepare directly for V-A.

sections.heading: Can you prepare for both together?
paragraphs: Yes. The V-B syllabus is essentially a subset of V-A, so a candidate who prepares properly for V-A will find V-B straightforward. The reverse is not true: V-B preparation alone leaves big gaps in regulation, taxation, scheme documents and performance measurement.

If you take V-B first, treat it as the foundation and reuse your notes. Then add the V-A-only chapters — especially Legal and Regulatory Framework, NAV, TER and Pricing, Taxation, and Scheme Selection — and practise numericals and situational questions, which V-B covers lightly.

sections.heading: A simple decision checklist
paragraphs: If you are still unsure after reading the comparison, answer the following questions honestly. Two or more 'yes' answers point clearly towards V-A.

Remember that the certificate is only one step. Registration with AMFI, KYD (know your distributor) formalities, empanelment with AMCs and continuing professional education are separate requirements, and their current procedures are published on amfiindia.com and nism.ac.in. Read those pages before you pay for either exam so that you know the full path from certificate to first transaction.
bullets: Will you be recommending equity or hybrid funds to clients in the next two years?
Does your employer's job description or appointment letter mention NISM V-A by name?
Are you planning to pursue investment adviser, PMS distribution or other advanced NISM certifications later?
Do you expect clients to ask about taxation, scheme selection or risk-adjusted returns?
Are you comfortable studying for around two to three weeks with a few timed practice tests?

sections.heading: Preparation time for each
paragraphs: Most candidates need around one week of steady study for V-B and about two to three weeks for V-A, depending on prior exposure to markets. For V-A, plan to sit a few full-length timed mock tests and spend time reviewing the explanations, because the 0.25 negative marking punishes careless guesses. For V-B, chapter-wise practice and one or two timed tests are usually enough.

Whichever you pick, download the current workbook from nism.ac.in, study from that edition, and confirm registration steps, validity and continuing education requirements on the official NISM and AMFI websites.

One practical tip applies to both exams: do not memorise from summaries alone. The questions are framed around the exact wording of the workbook, so a term such as 'expense ratio', 'exit load' or 'riskometer' needs to be understood as the workbook defines it. Reading the chapter, then practising questions and checking explanations, is the most reliable sequence.

faqs: Is NISM V-B easier than V-A?

Generally yes. V-B has fewer questions, a shorter duration, an introductory syllabus and no negative marking in the indicative pattern. V-A covers regulation, taxation, NAV calculations and scheme selection in far more depth and deducts marks for wrong answers, so it needs more practice.
Can I get an ARN with NISM V-B?

V-B is linked to a new-cadre distributor category that is allowed to sell only a limited set of simpler schemes, subject to SEBI and AMFI rules. For the regular ARN covering the full range of schemes, V-A is the standard certification. Confirm current eligibility on amfiindia.com before applying.
Should I take V-B before V-A?

It is optional. If you are entirely new to finance, V-B can be a gentle start, and its syllabus overlaps heavily with V-A. If you already know you want to sell the full product range, preparing directly for V-A saves time and an extra exam.

guides.title: How to Prepare for NISM Series VIII in 21 Days
guides.description: A 21-day NISM Series VIII preparation plan: week-by-week chapters, approximate weightage, options practice, revision schedule and timed mock tests.
guides.primary: how to prepare for nism series viii
secondary: how to pass nism series viii
guides.intro: Many candidates ask how to prepare for NISM Series VIII because it has a reputation as one of the tougher NISM papers. The Equity Derivatives exam combines definitions with numericals on futures pricing, option payoffs, margins and strategies, and the pass mark is higher than several other NISM exams. A three-week plan works well for most working professionals: it leaves enough time for the options chapters, which need practice rather than reading, and for several timed mock tests. This guide sets out the plan week by week, with approximate chapter weightage and a revision routine.

sections.heading: Know the pattern before you plan
paragraphs: The indicative pattern is 100 questions for 100 marks in 120 minutes, with a passing score of 60 percent and negative marking of 0.25 marks per wrong answer. These details are indicative — confirm in the latest official notification on nism.ac.in before you register, because NISM revises workbooks and exam structures periodically.

A 60 percent pass line with negative marking means you need around 65 to 70 correct answers with few wrong ones. That is achievable, but only if the calculation-based chapters are solid. Candidates who skip options pricing and strategies typically find themselves stuck in the mid-50s.

sections.heading: Is three weeks right for you?
paragraphs: Twenty-one days assumes about two hours on weekdays and three hours on weekends. If you already trade futures and options, you can compress Week 1 into three or four days and spend the saved time on extra mock tests. If you are new to markets altogether, stretch the plan to four weeks by giving Introduction to Options and the strategies chapter one more week each; these are the chapters where rushed preparation shows up most in scores.

Whatever your background, download the latest workbook from nism.ac.in and use it as the primary source. Lot sizes, margin frameworks and position limits are periodically revised by SEBI and the exchanges, and questions follow the workbook edition rather than older notes or videos.

sections.heading: Approximate chapter weightage
paragraphs: NISM does not publish an official mark split. Based on the syllabus and the length of workbook chapters, the following is an approximate guide to where questions tend to concentrate.
bullets: Heaviest: Introduction to Options (payoffs, moneyness, premium components, Greeks) and Strategies using Equity Futures and Options.
Heavy: Introduction to Forwards and Futures (cost of carry, basis, hedging with beta) and Trading Mechanism (order types, contract specifications, position limits).
Medium: Clearing and Settlement System (margins, mark-to-market, settlement of futures and options) and Legal and Regulatory Environment.
Lighter but scoring: Basics of Derivatives, Understanding Index, Accounting and Taxation, and Sales Practices and Investor Protection.

sections.heading: Week 1: foundations and futures
paragraphs: Use the first week to build vocabulary and get comfortable with futures, which are simpler than options and underpin everything that follows. Study about two hours a day and finish each day with chapter-wise practice questions.
bullets: Days 1–2: Basics of Derivatives — forwards, futures, options and swaps; participants (hedgers, speculators, arbitrageurs); exchange-traded vs OTC.
Day 3: Understanding Index — free-float market capitalisation, index construction, impact cost, index funds and ETFs.
Days 4–6: Introduction to Forwards and Futures — cost of carry model, fair value, basis and convergence, hedging a portfolio with index futures using beta, calendar spreads.
Day 7: Revision of Week 1 and a 40-question mixed practice set on these chapters.

sections.heading: Week 2: options and strategies
paragraphs: This is the most important week. Do not try to memorise payoff tables; draw them. For every strategy, sketch the payoff at expiry and write down the maximum profit, maximum loss and breakeven.
bullets: Days 8–10: Introduction to Options — calls and puts, intrinsic and time value, moneyness, put-call parity, factors affecting premium, and the Greeks (delta, gamma, theta, vega, rho) at a conceptual level.
Days 11–13: Strategies using Equity Futures and Options — protective put, covered call, bull and bear spreads, straddles, strangles, butterflies, and hedging with futures and options.
Day 14: First full-length timed mock test, followed by a careful review of every options and strategies question.

sections.heading: Week 3: mechanics, regulation and mocks
paragraphs: The final week covers the operational and regulatory chapters, which are fact-based and quicker to learn, and builds exam stamina through mock tests.
bullets: Day 15: Trading Mechanism — order types, contract specifications, position limits, trading workstation basics.
Day 16: Clearing and Settlement System — clearing members, initial and exposure margins, mark-to-market, final settlement, physical settlement of stock derivatives.
Day 17: Legal and Regulatory Environment, Accounting and Taxation, and Sales Practices and Investor Protection.
Day 18: Second full-length mock; review and update your error log.
Day 19: Re-solve all options and futures numericals you got wrong; third mock in the evening.
Day 20: Fourth mock, then revise formula sheet and margin concepts.
Day 21: Light revision only — formula sheet, error log, strategy breakevens. Sleep early.

sections.heading: Build a one-page formula sheet
paragraphs: Most Series VIII numericals rely on a short list of relationships. Keeping them on one page and revising daily from Week 2 onwards is the single most effective habit for this exam.
bullets: Futures fair value under cost of carry, and the meaning of basis.
Number of futures contracts needed to hedge a portfolio using its beta.
Intrinsic value and time value of calls and puts; put-call parity.
Breakeven, maximum profit and maximum loss for each standard strategy.
Mark-to-market calculation on a futures position over a few days.

sections.heading: How to use mock tests well
paragraphs: Full-length timed mock tests are where Series VIII preparation comes together, because they reveal whether you can switch between a conceptual question and a calculation without losing time. Sit each mock in a single 120-minute block and then review every explanation, including for questions you got right by luck.

Track your accuracy on attempted questions. If it is below about 80 percent, you are attempting too many uncertain questions; with a 60 percent pass line, discipline in skipping matters as much as knowledge.

sections.heading: Exam-day approach
paragraphs: Start with a quick pass through all 100 questions, answering the factual ones immediately. Mark numericals and long strategy questions for a second pass, when you can give them full attention. Use rough paper for every payoff question — sketching takes seconds and prevents sign errors on puts and short positions. Only guess where you have eliminated at least two options.

In the final 15 minutes, review marked questions in order of confidence: first those where you had eliminated two options, then those where you had eliminated one. Do not change an answer you were sure of earlier unless you spot a clear calculation error; second-guessing under time pressure usually lowers the score.

faqs: Is NISM Series VIII difficult?

It is one of the more demanding NISM exams because of its 60 percent pass mark, negative marking and calculation-based questions on futures, options and strategies. Candidates who practise payoffs and numericals rather than only reading the workbook generally find it manageable within three to four weeks.
Which chapters should I focus on for NISM VIII?

Based on the syllabus, Introduction to Options and Strategies using Equity Futures and Options usually carry the most questions, followed by Forwards and Futures and the Trading Mechanism chapter. Regulation, taxation and investor protection are lighter and fact-based, so revise them quickly but do not skip them.
Do I need a calculator for NISM Series VIII?

The test is computer-based and the calculations are generally simple arithmetic. Practise doing them quickly on rough paper. Check the current candidate instructions on nism.ac.in for what is allowed at the test centre, as rules on calculators can change.

guides.title: NISM Series VIII Toughest Chapters and How to Score
guides.description: The toughest NISM Series VIII chapters — options, strategies, futures pricing and margins — and practical techniques to score well on each of them.
secondary: how to score in nism series viii
guides.intro: Most candidates who fall short in Equity Derivatives lose marks in the same places, which is why knowing the NISM Series VIII toughest chapters in advance is so useful. The exam's indicative pattern — 100 questions, 120 minutes, a 60 percent pass mark and 0.25 negative marking (confirm in the latest official notification on nism.ac.in) — leaves little room for weak areas. This guide walks through the four chapters that trouble candidates most, explains why they are hard, and gives specific techniques to turn each into a scoring area.

sections.heading: Why some chapters feel harder
paragraphs: Series VIII questions fall into two kinds: factual recall and applied reasoning. Factual questions on trading rules, regulation or taxation are straightforward if you have read the workbook carefully. Applied questions — what is the payoff of this position, how many contracts are needed to hedge, what is the breakeven — require you to work through a small problem under time pressure.

The chapters below are dominated by applied questions. They are hard not because the maths is advanced (it is basic arithmetic) but because a single sign error or confusion between long and short positions produces a wrong answer that also appears among the options.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction to Options
paragraphs: This chapter is the heart of the exam. Candidates struggle with moneyness for puts, the split of premium into intrinsic and time value, put-call parity, and the direction in which each factor moves call and put prices. The Greeks add a further layer: you need to know what delta, gamma, theta, vega and rho measure, their typical ranges, and how they behave for in-the-money, at-the-money and out-of-the-money options.

How to score: make a two-column table — calls on the left, puts on the right — and fill in moneyness conditions, intrinsic value formula, and the effect of a rise in spot price, strike, volatility, time to expiry and interest rate. Revise it until you can reproduce it from memory. Then solve at least 30 option questions across chapter-wise practice sets.
bullets: A call is in the money when spot is above strike; a put when spot is below strike.
Intrinsic value can never be negative; time value tends to decay towards zero at expiry.
Higher volatility generally raises the premium of both calls and puts.

sections.heading: 2. Strategies using Equity Futures and Options
paragraphs: Strategy questions describe a combination — say, buying one call and selling another at a higher strike — and ask for maximum profit, maximum loss, breakeven or the market view the strategy expresses. Candidates who memorise names without understanding payoffs get confused when the question uses different strikes or quantities.

How to score: for every strategy, draw the expiry payoff on rough paper with the underlying price on the horizontal axis. Mark the strikes, then calculate profit or loss at a price below the lower strike, between strikes and above the higher strike. Three points are enough to see the shape and read off the answer.
bullets: Bull call spread and bull put spread: moderately bullish, limited profit and limited loss.
Long straddle and long strangle: expect a big move in either direction, loss limited to premium paid.
Short straddle: expects low volatility, loss potentially unlimited.
Protective put and covered call: combine a stock or futures position with an option to change the risk profile.

sections.heading: 3. Introduction to Forwards and Futures
paragraphs: The cost of carry model, basis, convergence at expiry and beta-based hedging are the trouble spots. Questions may give a spot price, interest rate, dividend and days to expiry and ask for the fair futures price, or give a portfolio value and beta and ask how many index futures contracts to sell.

How to score: practise the fair value calculation in both simple and continuous compounding forms if the current workbook uses both, and always check whether the dividend reduces the carry. For hedging, remember the logic: portfolio value multiplied by beta, divided by the value of one futures contract (futures price multiplied by lot size). Work through at least ten such problems.

sections.heading: 4. Clearing and Settlement System
paragraphs: This chapter is less about calculation and more about precise operational rules, which is why it surprises candidates. Questions test the types of margins, who collects them from whom, how daily mark-to-market settlement works, and how final settlement differs for index and stock derivatives.

How to score: draw the flow of money from the client to the trading member to the clearing member to the clearing corporation. Then work through a three-day mark-to-market example on a long futures position, writing down the daily settlement amount. Once you have done it by hand, MCQs on this topic become much easier.

sections.heading: Easier chapters you should not neglect
paragraphs: Because so much effort goes into the four tough chapters, candidates sometimes under-prepare the lighter ones and lose easy marks. These chapters are short, factual and quick to revise, so they offer some of the best marks-per-hour in the syllabus.
bullets: Basics of Derivatives: definitions, history, types of participants, exchange-traded versus OTC contracts.
Understanding Index: free-float methodology, impact cost, index maintenance and uses of an index.
Trading Mechanism: order types, contract specifications, position limits, and the role of trading members.
Legal and Regulatory Environment: the role of SEBI and the exchanges, and key regulatory provisions covered in the workbook.
Accounting and Taxation: accounting treatment of futures and options and the tax treatment of derivatives income as described in the current workbook edition.
Sales Practices and Investor Protection: suitability, risk disclosure and grievance redressal.

sections.heading: Turning weak areas into scoring areas
paragraphs: Spend roughly 60 percent of your total preparation time on these four chapters and 40 percent on the rest. That sounds lopsided, but the remaining chapters — Basics of Derivatives, Understanding Index, Trading Mechanism, Legal and Regulatory Environment, Accounting and Taxation, and Sales Practices and Investor Protection — are largely factual and respond well to two careful readings plus practice questions.

Use full-length timed mock tests to confirm progress. After each attempt, sort your mistakes by chapter. If options or strategies still dominate your error list, go back to drawing payoffs rather than re-reading theory. Reviewing the explanation for every wrong answer is what converts a 55 into a 65.
bullets: Keep an error log with the chapter, the concept and the one-line correction.
Re-attempt every wrong numerical a day later without looking at the solution.
Revise the formula sheet and the calls-vs-puts table every day in the final week.

sections.heading: Managing these chapters on exam day
paragraphs: On the day, do not let a long strategy question break your rhythm. Mark it, finish the factual questions first, and return with a fresh mind. When you do attempt it, sketch the payoff — it takes less than a minute and catches most errors. With negative marking, skip any applied question where you cannot narrow the options down to two.

faqs: Which is the toughest chapter in NISM Series VIII?

Most candidates find Introduction to Options and the strategies chapter the hardest, because they combine concepts like moneyness and the Greeks with payoff calculations. These chapters also tend to carry a large share of questions, so they deserve the most practice time.
How many numerical questions come in NISM Series VIII?

The number varies by paper and NISM does not publish a fixed count. Expect a meaningful share of questions on futures pricing, hedging, option payoffs, strategies and mark-to-market. The arithmetic is simple, but you need to practise to avoid sign and direction errors.
How can I improve my score in options strategies?

Draw the expiry payoff for every strategy instead of memorising names. Calculate profit or loss at three underlying prices — below, between and above the strikes — to find breakevens and limits. Then practise mixed strategy questions in timed conditions and review each explanation.

guides.title: How to Prepare for NISM Series X-A in 30 Days
guides.description: A 30-day NISM Series X-A study plan for Investment Adviser Level 1: weekly chapter schedule, approximate weightage, TVM practice, revision and mock tests.
guides.primary: how to prepare for nism series x-a
secondary: how to pass nism series x-a
guides.intro: Anyone working out how to prepare for NISM Series X-A quickly realises that the syllabus is broad. Investment Adviser Level 1 covers financial planning basics, time value of money, every major asset class, portfolio construction, behavioural finance, operations and the SEBI regulations for investment advisers. A 30-day plan gives a working professional enough time to read the workbook properly, practise the calculation chapters and sit several full-length tests. This guide lays out the plan week by week, with approximate chapter weightage, a revision routine and a mock-test schedule built around the three-hour exam.

sections.heading: The exam pattern and what it means
paragraphs: The indicative pattern is 100 questions for 100 marks in 180 minutes, with a pass mark of 60 percent and negative marking of 0.25 marks for each wrong answer. Treat these as indicative — confirm in the latest official notification on nism.ac.in, since NISM revises workbooks and exam structures.

Three hours for 100 questions suggests that a fair number of questions take more than a minute: case-style questions, time value of money calculations and portfolio return problems. The 60 percent pass line combined with negative marking means you cannot afford large gaps. The plan below therefore spreads effort across the whole syllabus rather than gambling on a few chapters.

sections.heading: Approximate chapter weightage
paragraphs: NISM does not publish an official chapter-wise split. The grouping below is approximate and based on the syllabus and the depth of each workbook chapter. Use it to plan revision time, not to drop chapters.
bullets: High: Time Value of Money; Equity Investment; Debt Investment; Mutual Funds; Asset Allocation & Portfolio Construction; Regulatory Framework for Investment Advisers.
Medium: Investment Advisory & Financial Planning Basics; Client Financial Position & Debt Management; Derivatives; Portfolio Performance Evaluation; Ethics, Conflicts & Grievance Redressal.

Lower but direct: Indian Financial Markets; Securities Market Segments; Real Estate, Gold & Other Assets; PMS, AIF & Other Managed Portfolios; Behavioural Finance; Operational Aspects (KYC, Demat, Transactions).
Calculation-heavy areas: TVM (future value, present value, annuities, EMI), bond yields and duration basics, portfolio returns and risk-adjusted measures.

sections.heading: Week 1: planning basics and the maths
paragraphs: Front-load the maths. Time value of money appears across the syllabus — in debt, retirement-style goal calculations and loan questions — so getting fluent early pays off for the rest of the month. Study two hours on weekdays and three to four hours on weekends.
bullets: Days 1–2: Investment Advisory & Financial Planning Basics — the planning process, client life cycle, goal setting, the role of an adviser.
Days 3–5: Time Value of Money — compounding, discounting, annuities, EMI, real vs nominal returns; solve at least 25 problems.
Day 6: Client Financial Position & Debt Management — personal balance sheet, cash flow statement, liquidity and debt ratios.
Day 7: Revise Week 1 and complete chapter-wise practice questions for all three chapters.

sections.heading: Week 2: markets and asset classes
paragraphs: Week 2 builds product knowledge. Questions often ask which product fits a particular investor, so note the risk, return, liquidity and tax features of each one as you go.
bullets: Day 8: Indian Financial Markets and Securities Market Segments — primary and secondary markets, money and debt markets, participants and regulators.
Days 9–10: Equity Investment — valuation basics, ratios, fundamental and technical analysis at an introductory level.
Days 11–12: Debt Investment — bond features, yield measures, price-yield relationship, duration, credit risk.
Day 13: Derivatives — futures and options basics, uses for hedging.
Day 14: Mutual Funds — structure, categories, costs, and how to evaluate schemes.

sections.heading: Week 3: portfolios, behaviour and regulation
paragraphs: This week shifts from products to how an adviser combines them and the rules that govern advice.
bullets: Day 15: Real Estate, Gold & Other Assets; PMS, AIF & Other Managed Portfolios.
Days 16–17: Asset Allocation & Portfolio Construction — strategic vs tactical allocation, rebalancing, diversification.
Day 18: Portfolio Performance Evaluation — absolute and annualised returns, Sharpe, Treynor and other measures covered in the workbook.
Day 19: Behavioural Finance — common biases and how they affect investor decisions.
Day 20: Operational Aspects — KYC, demat, transactions and documentation.
Days 21–22: Regulatory Framework for Investment Advisers and Ethics, Conflicts & Grievance Redressal — read twice, these are exact-wording chapters.

sections.heading: Week 4: mocks and revision
paragraphs: The final eight days are about consolidation. Take full-length timed mock tests in a single 180-minute sitting and review every explanation afterwards. The review usually takes as long as the test itself, and it is time well spent.
bullets: Day 23: First full-length mock and detailed review.
Day 24: Rework all TVM and portfolio numericals from your error log.
Day 25: Second mock; revise the regulatory chapter.
Day 26: Revise asset class comparison notes and behavioural finance.
Day 27: Third mock; update the error log.
Day 28: Revise weakest three chapters identified from mocks.
Day 29: Fourth mock or a mixed practice set of 50 questions.
Day 30: Light revision of formula sheet, regulatory notes and error log only.

sections.heading: Revision techniques that work for X-A
paragraphs: X-A mixes two kinds of memory: procedural (how to solve a TVM problem) and declarative (what the regulations say). Revise them differently. For procedures, re-solve problems without looking at worked answers. For regulations, write short summaries in your own words and then compare them against the workbook text to catch subtle differences.

Create a product comparison grid with rows for equity shares, bonds, mutual funds, gold, real estate, PMS and AIFs, and columns for risk, return potential, liquidity, minimum ticket size and typical investor. Many questions boil down to reading one row of that grid correctly.
bullets: Keep a single formula sheet for TVM, returns and ratios.
Revise the regulatory chapter on at least four separate days.
Maintain an error log and read it every evening in Week 4.

sections.heading: Common mistakes X-A candidates make
paragraphs: The most frequent mistake is treating X-A as a reading exam. The workbook is long, and candidates who read it once from start to finish without practising questions often score in the low 50s. The second is underestimating the regulatory chapter; questions on adviser obligations, segregation of advice and distribution, fee rules and record keeping are framed around exact provisions, and small wording differences decide the answer. Always read the version in the current workbook, as SEBI amends these regulations from time to time.

sections.heading: Exam-day time management
paragraphs: With 180 minutes, aim to finish the first pass in about 100 minutes, answering every question you are confident about and marking calculations and long case questions. Spend the next 60 minutes on marked questions and keep the last 20 minutes for a final review. Because of the 0.25 negative marking, guess only after eliminating at least two options. Remember that X-A is one of two certifications needed for investment adviser registration, so pace yourself for a good score rather than a narrow pass.

faqs: Is 30 days enough to prepare for NISM Series X-A?

For most candidates with a finance or commerce background who can study two to three hours daily, 30 days is a reasonable window. If TVM and bond maths are new to you, add a week. Those already working in wealth management may manage in three weeks with consistent mock practice.
Which chapters carry the most weight in NISM X-A?

Based on the syllabus, time value of money, equity and debt investment, mutual funds, asset allocation and the investment adviser regulations tend to carry the most questions. NISM does not publish an official split, so cover every chapter and use weightage only to prioritise revision.
How difficult is NISM Series X-A?

It is moderately difficult because of the breadth of the syllabus, the 60 percent pass mark in the indicative pattern and negative marking. The maths is not advanced, but it needs practice. Regular chapter-wise questions and a few full-length timed tests make the difficulty manageable.

guides.title: NISM X-A vs X-B: Investment Adviser Level 1 vs Level 2
guides.description: NISM X-A vs X-B compared: syllabus, difficulty, exam pattern, order of attempting and how to prepare for both investment adviser certifications.
secondary: difference between nism x-a and x-b
which is tougher nism x-a or x-b
nism x-a and x-b both required
guides.intro: If you are planning to register as an investment adviser, the NISM X-A vs X-B question is not really about choosing one — under the current framework you generally need both. What candidates actually want to know is how the two levels differ, which is harder, which to take first and how much of the preparation overlaps. This guide compares Investment Adviser Level 1 and Level 2 chapter by chapter, explains the indicative exam patterns and suggests a sensible order and timeline for clearing both.

sections.heading: Do you need both X-A and X-B?
paragraphs: For individuals seeking SEBI registration as an investment adviser, and for principal officers and persons associated with investment advice in a registered entity, the regulations have required certification in both levels. Requirements can change, so verify the current position on sebi.gov.in and the exam details on nism.ac.in before you plan.

Some candidates take only X-A first, for example to build credibility in a wealth management role, and add X-B later. That is perfectly reasonable, but if registration is your goal, plan for both from the start.

sections.heading: Pattern comparison
paragraphs: Both exams follow the same indicative pattern: 100 questions for 100 marks in 180 minutes, with a pass mark of 60 percent and negative marking of 0.25 for each wrong answer. Treat this as indicative — confirm in the latest official notification on nism.ac.in.

The identical structure means your exam-day technique transfers directly from one to the other. What changes is the content and the style of questions: X-A leans towards concepts and products, while X-B leans towards applying planning concepts to client situations.

sections.heading: What X-A (Level 1) covers
paragraphs: X-A builds the foundation an adviser needs. It is about understanding markets, products and portfolios, plus the rules that govern advice.
bullets: Investment advisory and financial planning basics, and the client's financial position and debt management.
Time value of money — compounding, discounting, annuities and loan calculations.
Indian financial markets and their segments; equity, debt, derivatives and mutual funds.
Real estate, gold and other assets; PMS, AIF and other managed portfolios.
Asset allocation, portfolio construction and performance evaluation.
Behavioural finance, operational aspects such as KYC and demat, the regulatory framework for investment advisers, and ethics and grievance redressal.

sections.heading: What X-B (Level 2) covers
paragraphs: X-B takes the adviser into comprehensive financial planning. It assumes you already understand the products and asks you to apply them to protection, retirement, tax and estate needs.
bullets: Risk management and insurance concepts; life, health and general insurance products; insurance needs analysis.
Retirement planning concepts, retirement products and pension schemes, and retirement corpus and distribution planning.
Income tax fundamentals and taxation of investment products.
Wealth management and estate planning concepts; wills, succession and trusts.
Comprehensive financial planning and case studies that pull these areas together.

sections.heading: Which is tougher?
paragraphs: Candidates are split, and it depends on background. Those from a markets or equity background usually find X-A comfortable and X-B harder, because insurance, retirement, tax and succession law are new territory. Those from insurance or tax backgrounds often find the reverse.

In general, X-B feels more demanding to many candidates because of two features: the taxation chapters require precise knowledge of rules that are revised through Finance Acts, and the case-study chapter asks you to combine several calculations — insurance need, retirement corpus, tax impact — in a single scenario. X-A has more breadth; X-B has more depth and application.

A useful self-test before deciding how to split your time: try ten mixed questions from each level's chapter-wise practice sets before starting serious preparation. The level where you score lower is the one that needs the longer runway, regardless of what other candidates say about difficulty.

sections.heading: Which should you take first?
paragraphs: Take X-A first. Its time value of money, asset class and portfolio chapters are the building blocks for X-B's retirement corpus calculations and case studies. Candidates who attempt X-B first often find themselves learning X-A concepts in a hurry anyway.

A practical sequence is to prepare for X-A for about four weeks, sit the exam, and begin X-B preparation within a week or two while TVM and product knowledge are still fresh. Allow four to five weeks for X-B, with more time on taxation and case studies.

sections.heading: How much of the preparation overlaps?
paragraphs: The overlap is mainly in skills rather than chapters. TVM, return calculations and product understanding from X-A are used constantly in X-B. Regulatory and ethics knowledge from X-A also helps you interpret adviser-client situations in X-B case studies.

Plan around 30 to 40 percent less effort on the shared foundations for X-B if you have just cleared X-A, and redirect that time to tax rules, insurance needs analysis, retirement distribution and estate planning tools such as wills, nomination and trusts.
bullets: Reuse your X-A formula sheet and extend it with retirement corpus and insurance need methods.
Start a fresh notes file for taxation, organised by product, because questions are often product-specific.
Practise case studies end to end rather than as isolated calculations.

sections.heading: A sample combined timeline
paragraphs: For a working professional studying around two to three hours a day, the following ten-week outline covers both certifications without burning out. Adjust it to your background: compress the X-A weeks if you already work in markets, or stretch the X-B weeks if tax and insurance are new to you.
bullets: Weeks 1–3: X-A chapters, with chapter-wise practice questions after each.
Week 4: X-A full-length mocks, revision and the exam.
Week 5: Break of a few days, then X-B insurance chapters.
Week 6: X-B retirement chapters, reusing your X-A TVM sheet.
Week 7: X-B taxation and estate planning chapters.
Week 8: X-B case studies.
Weeks 9–10: X-B full-length mocks, revision and the exam.

sections.heading: Mock tests for both levels
paragraphs: For both exams, take several full-length timed mock tests in the final week and spend time reviewing explanations, especially for questions that took longer than two minutes. In X-A, the reviews usually reveal gaps in TVM or regulation; in X-B, they tend to reveal gaps in tax rules or in the sequence of steps in a case. Track accuracy on attempted questions, and skip rather than guess when you cannot eliminate at least two options.

Finally, keep the two sets of notes separate but cross-referenced. When an X-B case study uses a concept from X-A — say, real rate of return or the price-yield relationship of bonds — add a short pointer to the relevant X-A page. This turns your notes into a single reference for advisory work after the exams, which is ultimately the purpose of both certifications.

faqs: Can I take NISM X-B before X-A?

Check the current rules on nism.ac.in, as eligibility conditions can change. Even where it is permitted, X-A first is the more logical order, because X-B's retirement and case-study questions build directly on X-A's time value of money, asset class and portfolio concepts.
Is X-B harder than X-A?

Many candidates find X-B harder because of taxation, insurance needs analysis, retirement corpus calculations and integrated case studies. X-A covers a broader range of topics but at a more conceptual level. Your own background in markets, insurance or tax will influence which feels tougher.
How long does it take to clear both X-A and X-B?

A working professional studying two to three hours a day typically needs about four weeks for X-A and four to five weeks for X-B, so roughly two to two and a half months in total. Keeping the gap between the two exams short helps retain the shared foundations.

guides.title: How to Prepare for NISM Series X-B in 30 Days
guides.description: A 30-day NISM Series X-B plan for Investment Adviser Level 2: weekly schedule for insurance, retirement, tax and estate planning, revision and mock tests.
guides.primary: how to prepare for nism series x-b
secondary: how to pass nism series x-b
guides.intro: Once Level 1 is behind you, the next question is how to prepare for NISM Series X-B efficiently. Investment Adviser Level 2 is about comprehensive financial planning: insurance and risk management, retirement planning, income tax and taxation of investment products, estate planning and integrated case studies. It rewards application more than recall. A 30-day plan suits most working candidates and allows enough time for the tax chapters and case-study practice. This guide gives a week-by-week schedule, approximate chapter weightage, revision techniques and a mock-test routine for the three-hour exam.

sections.heading: Pattern and approach
paragraphs: The indicative pattern is 100 questions carrying 100 marks in 180 minutes, with a pass mark of 60 percent and 0.25 negative marking per wrong answer. Treat this as indicative — confirm in the latest official notification on nism.ac.in.

Because X-B includes case-based questions that require several steps, the 180-minute duration is useful but not lavish. Candidates who know the concepts but have not practised multi-step problems often run short of time in the last third of the paper. The plan below therefore starts case practice early rather than leaving it to the final week.

It also helps to remember the purpose of the certification. X-B tests whether you can build a sensible plan for a real household, so while studying each chapter, ask yourself how you would explain the concept to a client in two sentences. If you cannot, the concept is not yet clear enough for an applied question.

sections.heading: Approximate chapter weightage
paragraphs: There is no official chapter-wise mark split. Based on the syllabus and the depth of each workbook chapter, the following grouping is approximate.
bullets: High: Comprehensive Financial Planning & Case Studies; Taxation of Investment Products; Retirement Corpus & Distribution Planning; Insurance Needs Analysis.
Medium: Income Tax Fundamentals; Life Insurance Products; Retirement Products & Pension Schemes; Wills, Succession & Trusts.
Lower but direct: Risk Management & Insurance Concepts; Health & General Insurance; Retirement Planning Concepts; Wealth Management & Estate Planning Concepts.
Calculation-heavy areas: human life value and need-based insurance methods, retirement corpus and annuity calculations, capital gains and tax computation on investments.

sections.heading: Week 1: insurance and risk
paragraphs: Start with insurance because it introduces the needs-based thinking used throughout X-B. Study about two hours on weekdays and three to four hours on weekends, ending each day with chapter-wise practice questions.
bullets: Days 1–2: Risk Management & Insurance Concepts — risk identification, risk retention vs transfer, principles of insurance.
Days 3–4: Life Insurance Products — term, endowment, ULIPs, annuities; features and suitability.
Day 5: Health & General Insurance — indemnity vs benefit plans, key policy terms, property and liability cover.
Day 6: Insurance Needs Analysis — human life value and need-based methods; solve at least 15 problems.
Day 7: Revision and a mixed practice set on Week 1 chapters.

sections.heading: Week 2: retirement planning
paragraphs: Retirement questions draw heavily on time value of money from X-A. Revise your TVM formula sheet on Day 8 before starting.
bullets: Day 8: TVM refresher and Retirement Planning Concepts — accumulation and distribution phases, inflation, life expectancy.
Days 9–10: Retirement Products & Pension Schemes — employer-linked and voluntary schemes covered in the workbook, annuity options.
Days 11–13: Retirement Corpus & Distribution Planning — estimating expenses at retirement, corpus required, savings needed per year, withdrawal strategies.
Day 14: First full-length timed mock test and a detailed review.

sections.heading: Week 3: tax and estate planning
paragraphs: Tax rules are revised through Finance Acts, so study only from the current workbook edition on nism.ac.in and note the assessment year it refers to.
bullets: Days 15–16: Income Tax Fundamentals — heads of income, residential status, deductions and the regimes as described in the workbook.
Days 17–18: Taxation of Investment Products — capital gains on equity, debt, mutual funds, property and gold; tax treatment of interest, dividends and insurance proceeds.
Day 19: Wealth Management & Estate Planning Concepts.
Day 20: Wills, Succession & Trusts — types of wills, succession under personal laws at the level covered in the workbook, nomination vs inheritance, private trusts.
Day 21: Second full-length mock and review.

sections.heading: Week 4: case studies and mocks
paragraphs: The final stretch is about integration. Case studies combine insurance, retirement, tax and estate concepts for one client, so practise them in full rather than as isolated sub-questions.
bullets: Days 22–23: Comprehensive Financial Planning & Case Studies — work through every case in the workbook, writing out each step.
Day 24: Third mock; add mistakes to the error log.
Day 25: Revise tax rules product by product.
Day 26: Re-solve all insurance and retirement numericals from the error log.
Day 27: Fourth mock and review.
Days 28–29: Revise weakest chapters and estate planning notes.
Day 30: Light revision of formula sheet, tax table and error log.

sections.heading: Revision tips specific to X-B
paragraphs: Build a tax table with one row per product — equity shares, equity funds, debt funds, bonds, fixed deposits, gold, property, insurance policies — and columns for holding period rules, rate treatment and exemptions as given in the current workbook. Most tax questions can be answered by reading one row.

For case studies, write a fixed sequence on the first page of your notes: understand the client's goals, compute insurance gap, compute retirement gap, consider tax implications, then consider estate issues. Following the same sequence every time saves minutes in the exam.
bullets: Practise insurance need and retirement corpus calculations until each takes under three minutes.
Review full-length mock explanations in detail, especially for case questions.
Read the wills and succession chapter twice for terminology.

sections.heading: Who needs a longer plan
paragraphs: Thirty days works for candidates who have recently cleared X-A and still remember time value of money. If more than a few months have passed since Level 1, add three to four days at the start purely for TVM and portfolio return revision. If you have never studied income tax, add another week to Block 3; the tax chapters cover many products and rules, and questions test specifics such as holding periods and the treatment of different kinds of income. Those already working in insurance or tax advisory can shorten the corresponding week and invest the time in additional case-study practice, which tends to be the deciding factor between a narrow miss and a comfortable pass.

sections.heading: Exam-day strategy
paragraphs: Do a first pass of about 90 minutes answering direct questions and short calculations. Use the next 70 minutes for case studies and longer numericals, and keep 20 minutes to review. With negative marking, attempt a doubtful question only after eliminating at least two options. If a case-study set looks long, read all its sub-questions first; often one or two can be answered without the full calculation.

faqs: Is 30 days enough for NISM Series X-B?

For most candidates who have recently cleared X-A and can study two to three hours a day, 30 days is realistic. Those without exposure to taxation or insurance should allow five to six weeks, giving extra time to tax rules, retirement corpus calculations and case-study practice.
Which chapters are most important in NISM X-B?

Based on the syllabus, comprehensive financial planning and case studies, taxation of investment products, retirement corpus planning and insurance needs analysis tend to carry the most weight. NISM does not publish an official split, so cover every chapter and use this only for prioritising.
Do I need to clear X-A before attempting X-B?

Check the current eligibility rules on nism.ac.in, as these can change. Regardless of rules, preparing for X-A first is sensible because X-B's retirement and case-study questions use X-A's time value of money, product and portfolio concepts throughout.

guides.title: NISM Series X-B Syllabus Explained Chapter by Chapter
guides.description: NISM Series X-B syllabus explained chapter by chapter: what each Investment Adviser Level 2 topic covers, typical question styles and what to focus on.
guides.intro: The NISM Series X-B syllabus looks short on paper — a dozen or so chapters — but each one goes deep into a part of personal financial planning. Investment Adviser Level 2 moves from knowing products to advising on protection, retirement, tax and succession for a real client. This guide explains the syllabus chapter by chapter in the order most candidates study it, describes what each chapter actually tests, and points out where questions tend to be factual and where they become applied. Use it alongside the current workbook from nism.ac.in, which remains the authoritative source.

sections.heading: How the syllabus is organised
paragraphs: The chapters fall into five blocks: insurance and risk management, retirement planning, taxation, estate planning, and comprehensive planning through case studies. The first four blocks build knowledge; the fifth tests whether you can combine them. The indicative exam pattern is 100 questions for 100 marks in 180 minutes, with a 60 percent pass mark and 0.25 negative marking — indicative, so confirm in the latest official notification on nism.ac.in.
The chapter names below follow the topics in the current syllabus as we understand it. NISM revises workbooks periodically, so check the edition and its effective date before you begin.

sections.heading: Block 1: insurance and risk management
paragraphs: Risk Management & Insurance Concepts introduces how risks are identified and handled — avoidance, reduction, retention and transfer — and the core principles of insurance such as insurable interest, utmost good faith, indemnity and subrogation. Questions here are mostly definitional and reward careful reading.

Life Insurance Products covers term plans, endowment and money-back policies, whole life, ULIPs and annuities. Expect questions on product features and on which product suits a described client, for example a young earner with dependants who needs maximum cover at minimum cost.

Health & General Insurance explains indemnity-based and benefit-based health covers, key terms such as waiting periods, co-payment and sub-limits, and property, motor and liability insurance at the level an adviser needs.

Insurance Needs Analysis is the first calculation-heavy chapter. It covers the human life value approach and need-based approaches, and asks you to work out how much cover a client requires. Practise these until you can complete one in a few minutes.

sections.heading: Block 2: retirement planning
paragraphs: Retirement Planning Concepts sets the stage: the accumulation and distribution phases, the effect of inflation and longevity, and the replacement-ratio idea of estimating expenses after retirement. Questions are conceptual but often include a short numerical.

Retirement Products & Pension Schemes describes the employer-linked and voluntary retirement products covered in the workbook, along with annuity options. Learn the features, contribution and withdrawal rules as the workbook states them, and verify any rules that may have changed since publication.

Retirement Corpus & Distribution Planning is the second major calculation chapter. You estimate expenses at retirement, compute the corpus needed to fund them for the expected retirement period, and work out how much the client must save each year. It relies heavily on time value of money from X-A.

sections.heading: Block 3: taxation
paragraphs: Income Tax Fundamentals covers residential status, heads of income, computation of total income, common deductions and the tax regimes as described in the workbook. Questions test whether you can classify income correctly and apply basic rules.

Taxation of Investment Products is one of the most important chapters. It explains how gains and income from equity shares, mutual funds, bonds, deposits, gold, real estate and insurance policies are taxed. Because tax law changes through annual Finance Acts, rely only on the current workbook edition and note the year it refers to. A product-by-product tax table is the most efficient way to revise this chapter.

sections.heading: Block 4: estate planning
paragraphs: Wealth Management & Estate Planning Concepts explains the objectives of estate planning — orderly transfer of wealth, minimising disputes, providing for dependants — and the tools available.

Wills, Succession & Trusts covers the essentials of a valid will, types of wills, probate, the broad framework of succession at the level covered in the workbook, the difference between nomination and inheritance, and the use of private trusts. This chapter is full of terminology, so careful reading matters more than calculation.

sections.heading: Block 5: comprehensive financial planning and case studies
paragraphs: This chapter ties everything together. A case describes a client — age, income, expenses, family, assets, liabilities, goals — followed by several questions. You may be asked to identify the insurance gap, estimate retirement savings needed, assess the tax effect of a recommendation or point out an estate planning issue.

Case questions are where most time is spent in the exam. Read all sub-questions before calculating, because some can be answered from the facts alone. Practise every case in the workbook, then take full-length timed mock tests to get used to switching between short and long questions.
bullets: Underline each number in the case as you use it, so you do not reuse or miss data.
Write intermediate results on rough paper; later sub-questions often build on them.
If a calculation result does not match any option, recheck inflation and the number of years before redoing everything.

sections.heading: How X-B questions are typically framed
paragraphs: Knowing the style of questions helps you study each chapter the right way. Broadly, X-B questions fall into four types, and each block of the syllabus leans towards one or two of them.
bullets: Definition questions: what a term means — for example indemnity, probate or annuity — common in the insurance and estate planning blocks.
Suitability questions: which product or approach fits a described client — common in life insurance, retirement products and wealth management.
Calculation questions: insurance need, retirement corpus, annual savings required or tax on a gain — common in needs analysis, retirement corpus and taxation chapters.
Case-based sets: a client profile followed by several linked questions drawing on all blocks.

sections.heading: Where to focus your preparation
paragraphs: Based on the syllabus, the case studies, taxation of investment products, retirement corpus planning and insurance needs analysis tend to carry the most weight and deserve the most practice. The concept chapters on insurance, retirement and estate planning are shorter and quicker to master, but they supply easy marks and should be read at least twice.

Combine chapter-wise practice questions after each block with three or four full-length mock tests in the final ten days, and review every explanation carefully. That pairing exposes both knowledge gaps and timing problems before the actual exam.

A practical rhythm is one block per week for four weeks, followed by a final week focused only on case studies and mocks. Keep a separate page of terms for the estate planning chapter and a separate page of formulas for insurance and retirement, and read both every day in the last week.

faqs: How many chapters are there in the NISM X-B syllabus?

The current syllabus covers roughly a dozen topics grouped into insurance, retirement planning, taxation, estate planning and comprehensive planning with case studies. NISM revises workbooks periodically, so download the latest edition from nism.ac.in and check its chapter list before you start.
Which part of the X-B syllabus is hardest?

Most candidates find taxation of investment products and the comprehensive case studies hardest. Taxation needs precise, current rules, and case studies require combining insurance, retirement and tax calculations for one client. Regular practice on full cases is the best way to build confidence.
Does the X-B syllabus include calculations?

Yes. Insurance needs analysis, retirement corpus and savings calculations, and tax on investment income all involve arithmetic, often using time value of money concepts from X-A. The maths is not advanced, but it needs practice to complete within the time available.

guides.title: How to Prepare for NISM Series XV in 30 Days
guides.description: A 30-day NISM Series XV Research Analyst study plan: weekly schedule, approximate weightage, valuation and ratio practice, revision and mock tests.
guides.primary: how to prepare for nism series xv
secondary: how to pass nism series xv
guides.intro: If you are figuring out how to prepare for NISM Series XV, start by accepting that it is a substantive exam. The Research Analyst certification covers the securities market, economic and industry analysis, company analysis, financial statements, valuation, risk and return, report writing and the SEBI research analyst regulations. It has a higher pass mark than many NISM papers and plenty of applied questions on ratios and valuation. A 30-day plan suits most working professionals. This guide sets out a week-by-week schedule, approximate chapter weightage, a revision approach and a mock-test routine for the three-hour exam.

sections.heading: Exam pattern and what it implies
paragraphs: The indicative pattern is 100 questions for 100 marks in 180 minutes, with a pass mark of 60 percent and negative marking of 0.25 marks per wrong answer. These are indicative — confirm in the latest official notification on nism.ac.in before registering.

The three-hour window reflects the number of applied questions: computing a ratio from given financial data, choosing an appropriate valuation method, or interpreting an economic indicator. You will need roughly 65 or more correct answers with few errors, so the plan gives real time to financial analysis and valuation rather than treating them as reading chapters.

sections.heading: Approximate chapter weightage
paragraphs: NISM does not publish an official chapter-wise split. Based on the syllabus and the depth of workbook chapters, this grouping is approximate.
bullets: High: Company Analysis – Financial Analysis; Corporate Valuation; Company Analysis – Business & Governance; Industry Analysis.
Medium: Economic Analysis; Fundamentals of Research; Fundamentals of Risk and Return; Legal and Regulatory Environment; Terminology in Equity and Debt Markets.
Lower but direct: Introduction to Research Analyst Profession; Introduction to Securities Market; Qualities of a Good Research Report.
Calculation-heavy areas: profitability, liquidity, leverage and efficiency ratios; DCF and relative valuation; return, standard deviation and beta.

sections.heading: Who should allow more time
paragraphs: Thirty days assumes about two hours on weekdays and three to four hours on weekends. Chartered accountants, CFA candidates and MBA finance graduates often need less time on financial analysis and can finish in three weeks. Engineers, sales professionals or anyone without accounting exposure should allow five to six weeks, because reading a balance sheet and cash flow statement fluently is a prerequisite for half the syllabus.
Whatever your background, use the current workbook from nism.ac.in as your primary source, particularly for the regulatory chapter, which follows the SEBI research analyst regulations as amended.

sections.heading: Week 1: the profession and the market
paragraphs: The first week builds context. These chapters are lighter, so use spare time to refresh accounting basics if needed.
bullets: Day 1: Introduction to Research Analyst Profession — role of sell-side and buy-side analysts, qualities, ethics.
Day 2: Introduction to Securities Market — primary and secondary markets, participants, instruments.
Day 3: Terminology in Equity and Debt Markets — corporate actions, market capitalisation, yields and bond terms.
Days 4–5: Fundamentals of Research — fundamental vs technical vs quantitative research, top-down and bottom-up approaches, sources of information.
Day 6: Economic Analysis — GDP, inflation, interest rates, fiscal and monetary policy, and their link to markets.
Day 7: Revision and chapter-wise practice questions for Week 1.

sections.heading: Week 2: industry and company analysis
paragraphs: This week covers how analysts judge a business before the numbers. Questions often describe a situation and ask which framework applies.
bullets: Days 8–9: Industry Analysis — industry life cycle, Porter's five forces, competitive structure, key industry metrics.
Days 10–11: Company Analysis – Business & Governance — business model, competitive advantage, management quality, corporate governance red flags.
Days 12–14: Company Analysis – Financial Analysis — reading the three statements, common-size analysis, ratio analysis, DuPont, cash flow quality. Solve at least 30 ratio problems.

sections.heading: Week 3: valuation, risk and reports
paragraphs: Valuation is the hardest technical part of the exam. Work every example in the workbook by hand before moving to practice questions.
bullets: Days 15–17: Corporate Valuation — DCF (FCFF and FCFE concepts), dividend discount model, relative valuation using P/E, EV/EBITDA, P/B and other multiples covered in the workbook.
Day 18: Fundamentals of Risk and Return — return measures, standard deviation, beta, CAPM.
Day 19: Qualities of a Good Research Report — structure, disclosures, clarity, avoiding bias.
Days 20–21: Legal and Regulatory Environment — SEBI research analyst regulations, conflicts of interest, disclosures, record keeping. Read twice.

sections.heading: Week 4: mocks and revision
paragraphs: Take full-length timed mock tests in a single 180-minute sitting and review every explanation carefully. Reviewing is where you discover whether a wrong valuation answer came from a concept gap or an arithmetic slip.
bullets: Day 22: First full-length mock and review.
Day 23: Rework all ratio and valuation errors.
Day 24: Second mock; revise regulations.
Day 25: Revise industry and governance frameworks.
Day 26: Third mock and error log update.
Days 27–28: Weakest chapters from mocks.
Day 29: Fourth mock or a mixed set of 50 questions.
Day 30: Light revision of formula sheet, regulatory notes and error log.

sections.heading: Revision habits that help
paragraphs: Keep a formula sheet with every ratio grouped by type — profitability, liquidity, leverage, efficiency, valuation — and write a one-line interpretation next to each, such as 'higher interest coverage means lower default risk'. Many questions test interpretation, not just computation.

For the regulatory chapter, write each obligation as a short question and answer card. Revise the cards on at least four separate days; exact provisions are easy to blur between this exam and other advisory certifications.

Practise valuation with real annual reports as well as workbook examples. Pick two listed companies from different industries, extract a few years of revenue, operating profit, debt and cash flow, and calculate the main ratios yourself. Then compare them with each other and ask what explains the differences. This exercise takes an evening, but it turns abstract formulas into something you can reason about, which is exactly what applied questions test.
bullets: Maintain an error log with the chapter, the concept and a one-line correction.
Re-solve every valuation question you got wrong a day later without looking at the solution.
Revise the economic indicators and their typical effect on interest-sensitive and export-oriented sectors.

sections.heading: Exam-day approach
paragraphs: Finish a first pass in about 100 minutes, answering direct questions and short calculations, and mark lengthy valuation or ratio sets. Use the next hour for marked questions and keep 20 minutes for review. Guess only after eliminating at least two options, given the 0.25 negative marking.

Keep in mind that the certificate is one part of the path to practising as a research analyst. Registration requirements, qualifications and continuing obligations are set by SEBI and may change, so check sebi.gov.in and nism.ac.in for the current position before you plan your career around the exam date.

faqs: Is NISM Series XV tough?

It is among the more demanding NISM exams because of its broad syllabus, the 60 percent pass mark in the indicative pattern, negative marking and applied questions on financial analysis and valuation. Candidates with an accounting or finance background usually find it manageable with three to four weeks of steady practice.
Which chapters are most important for NISM XV?

Based on the syllabus, company financial analysis, corporate valuation, business and governance analysis, and industry analysis tend to carry the most weight. Economic analysis, risk and return, and the regulatory chapter follow. NISM does not publish an official split, so cover every chapter.
Do I need an accounting background for NISM XV?

It helps a great deal, but it is not essential. If you are new to accounting, spend a few extra days learning to read a balance sheet, profit and loss statement and cash flow statement before starting the financial analysis chapter. That foundation makes ratios and valuation far easier.

guides.title: NISM Series XV Exam Strategy and Time Management
guides.description: NISM Series XV exam strategy: how to split 180 minutes, handle valuation and ratio questions, manage negative marking and review answers well on test day.
secondary: nism series xv exam day tips
how to attempt nism research analyst exam
guides.intro: Plenty of well-prepared candidates fall just short in the Research Analyst exam, not because they lack knowledge but because they run out of time or lose marks to careless guesses. A clear NISM Series XV exam strategy fixes both problems. The paper mixes quick factual questions with longer ratio, valuation and case-style questions, and the indicative pattern carries negative marking. This guide explains how to split the 180 minutes, the order in which to attack question types, how to handle calculations under pressure and how to decide when to guess and when to skip.

sections.heading: Start from the pattern
paragraphs: The indicative pattern is 100 questions carrying 100 marks in 180 minutes, with a pass mark of 60 percent and negative marking of 0.25 marks for each wrong answer. Confirm these details in the latest official notification on nism.ac.in, as NISM revises exams periodically.

Two conclusions follow. First, the average time per question is 1.8 minutes, but that average hides a wide spread: a terminology question takes 20 seconds while a valuation question can take four minutes. Second, at 0.25 per wrong answer, four wrong guesses cost one full mark. A good strategy maximises correct answers while keeping wrong ones low.

sections.heading: A three-pass plan for 180 minutes
paragraphs: Rather than answering strictly in order, move through the paper in three passes. This prevents a single difficult calculation from eating into time meant for easy marks later.
