bullets: Pass 1 (about 90 minutes): answer every question you can solve confidently in under two minutes — terminology, regulation, frameworks, short ratio questions. Mark everything else.
Pass 2 (about 65 minutes): return to marked questions, starting with calculations you know how to do, then those requiring interpretation.
Pass 3 (about 25 minutes): review marked-but-unanswered questions and decide whether to attempt or skip; check that no intended answer was left blank.

sections.heading: Handling ratio and financial analysis questions
paragraphs: Financial analysis questions usually give a few figures from the balance sheet or profit and loss statement and ask for a ratio or an interpretation. The trap is often in the definition — for example, whether a ratio uses total debt or long-term debt, or average or closing equity, as defined in the workbook.

Before calculating, write the formula on rough paper. Then substitute the numbers. This adds a few seconds but prevents the most common error, which is using the wrong denominator. If two options are close, recheck the definition rather than the arithmetic.
bullets: Profitability ratios: watch whether margins use revenue or net sales.
Leverage ratios: confirm which debt figure the definition uses.
DuPont questions: multiply the components; do not add them.
Interpretation questions: a higher or lower ratio is only 'good' in context — read the question carefully.

sections.heading: Handling valuation questions
paragraphs: Valuation questions are the longest in the paper. Typical ones ask for a value using the dividend discount model, the present value of projected cash flows, or a price implied by a peer multiple. Some are conceptual — which model suits a company with no dividends, or why EV-based multiples help compare firms with different capital structures.

Do the conceptual ones in Pass 1; they are quick if you have studied the chapter. Leave multi-step calculations for Pass 2. When you attempt them, estimate the answer roughly first. If your detailed calculation lands far from the estimate, you have probably mixed up the growth rate and the discount rate or missed a year in the discounting.

sections.heading: Negative marking: when to guess
paragraphs: A simple rule works well. If you can eliminate two of the four options, guessing between the remaining two has a positive expected value, and you should usually attempt it. If you can eliminate only one, or none, skip it unless time remains at the very end and you have a genuine reason to prefer one option.

Track this in your practice. In each full-length timed mock test, note how many guesses you made and how many were correct. If your guesses are right less than about 40 percent of the time, tighten your rule; if they are right more than 60 percent, you can afford to be a little bolder.

sections.heading: Regulation and report-writing questions
paragraphs: The legal and regulatory chapter and the chapter on qualities of a good research report produce some of the fastest marks in the paper, but only if you have read them closely. Questions often hinge on a single word — 'shall' versus 'may', a disclosure that is mandatory versus one that is recommended.

Answer these in Pass 1 and do not overthink them. If two options look correct, choose the one closest to the workbook's own phrasing. Second-guessing regulatory questions in Pass 3 tends to replace right answers with wrong ones.

sections.heading: Practising the strategy before exam day
paragraphs: Strategy only works if you have rehearsed it. Take at least three full-length timed mock tests in the last ten days, each in a single 180-minute sitting, and follow the three-pass plan exactly. After each test, review explanations for every wrong and every guessed question, and note how long each pass took.

Adjust the time split based on the results. If Pass 1 regularly runs over 100 minutes, you are spending too long on questions you should mark. If you finish Pass 2 with 40 minutes spare, you can afford to attempt more calculations in Pass 1.
bullets: Record score, attempts, accuracy and time per pass for each mock.
Keep a list of question types that regularly take you more than three minutes.
Practise those types separately in chapter-wise sets until they become routine.

sections.heading: Mistakes that cost marks
paragraphs: Reviewing mock results across many candidates shows the same handful of avoidable errors. Each one is cheap to fix once you know to look for it.
bullets: Spending five or more minutes on a single valuation question in the first pass.
Using closing instead of average figures (or the reverse) when the workbook definition specifies one.
Confusing the cost of equity with the overall cost of capital in discounting questions.
Changing correct regulatory answers in the final review without a clear reason.
Leaving questions unanswered that were solved on rough paper but never clicked on screen.

sections.heading: On the day itself
paragraphs: Reach the test centre early with the identification documents specified in your admit details, and read the on-screen instructions carefully before starting the timer. Use rough sheets generously — write formulas, intermediate results and question numbers you have marked. Glance at the clock at roughly 90 and 155 minutes to check you are on schedule. If panic sets in over a hard question, move on; there are easier marks elsewhere in the paper.

faqs: How should I divide time in the NISM XV exam?

A three-pass approach works well: around 90 minutes for questions you can answer confidently, about 65 minutes for marked calculations and interpretation questions, and roughly 25 minutes for final review. Adjust the split after practising it in full-length timed mock tests.
Should I attempt every question in NISM Series XV?

Not necessarily. The indicative pattern deducts 0.25 marks for each wrong answer. Attempt a question when you can eliminate at least two options. Skip questions where you would be guessing blindly, unless you have spare time and a genuine reason to prefer one option.
What are the most time-consuming questions in NISM XV?

Multi-step valuation questions, such as discounting projected cash flows or applying the dividend discount model, and ratio questions built on several financial statement figures usually take the longest. Leaving them for a second pass protects time for quicker, scoring questions.

guides.title: How to Prepare for NISM Series VII in 15 Days
guides.description: A 15-day NISM Series VII study plan for Securities Operations and Risk Management: daily chapters, approximate weightage, revision and timed mock tests.
guides.primary: how to prepare for nism series vii
secondary: how to pass nism series vii
guides.intro: If you work in a broker's back office or are about to, you will soon need to know how to prepare for NISM Series VII. Securities Operations and Risk Management tests the operational core of the stock market: market participants, broking operations, margins and risk management, clearing, settlement, investor grievances and other services provided by brokers. It is more process-driven than calculation-heavy, which makes a focused 15-day plan realistic for most working professionals. This guide gives a day-by-day schedule, approximate chapter weightage, a revision method and a mock-test routine.

sections.heading: Exam pattern at a glance
paragraphs: The indicative pattern is 100 questions for 100 marks in 120 minutes, with a pass mark of 50 percent and negative marking of 0.25 marks per wrong answer. Treat these as indicative — confirm in the latest official notification on nism.ac.in.

Two hours is ample for the number of questions, because most are factual or short process questions. The real challenge is precision: settlement cycles, margin types, the sequence of steps in pay-in and pay-out, and who is responsible for what. Negative marking punishes the 'I think it's this one' style of answering, so build clear, confident recall.

sections.heading: Is 15 days right for you?
paragraphs: The plan assumes about two hours on weekdays and a little more at weekends. If you already work in broking operations, many chapters will feel familiar and you could compress the first five days into three, using the time for an extra mock test. If you have never worked in the securities industry, stretch the plan to about three weeks: give two extra days to risk management and settlement, which are the most process-heavy chapters, and one extra day to broking operations.

Before you start, download the current workbook from nism.ac.in and check its effective date. Settlement cycles, margin frameworks and grievance procedures have all been revised in recent years, and questions follow the workbook edition rather than older notes or videos. Studying from an outdated source is one of the most common reasons well-prepared candidates still lose marks in this exam.

It also helps to keep the purpose of the exam in mind. Series VII is meant to make sure operations staff can handle client money and securities correctly. When you study a process, imagine yourself performing it at your desk; asking 'what would I check next?' makes sequences far easier to remember than rote reading.

sections.heading: Approximate chapter weightage
paragraphs: There is no official chapter-wise mark split. Based on the syllabus and the length of each workbook chapter, the following grouping is approximate.
bullets: High: Risk Management; Clearing Process; Settlement Process.
Medium: Introduction to Securities Broking Operations; Market Participants in the Securities Market; Investor Grievances and Arbitration.
Lower but direct: Introduction to the Securities Market; Other Services Provided by Brokers.
Numerical questions, where they appear, usually involve margins, mark-to-market, obligations or basic settlement amounts.

sections.heading: Days 1–5: market structure and broking operations
paragraphs: Study about two hours a day. Read the workbook chapter, write a one-page summary and finish with chapter-wise practice questions.
bullets: Day 1: Introduction to the Securities Market — primary and secondary markets, products, regulators, market infrastructure institutions.
Day 2: Market Participants in the Securities Market — exchanges, clearing corporations, depositories, brokers, custodians, banks and their roles.
Days 3–4: Introduction to Securities Broking Operations — client onboarding, KYC, account opening documents, order management, contract notes, trading terminals.
Day 5: Revision of Days 1–4 and a mixed practice set.

sections.heading: Days 6–10: risk, clearing and settlement
paragraphs: These three chapters are the heart of the exam. Draw flowcharts as you study; operations questions are much easier when you can picture the flow of funds and securities.
bullets: Days 6–7: Risk Management — types of margins, margin collection and reporting, mark-to-market, position limits, surveillance and risk containment measures.
Day 8: Clearing Process — the role of the clearing corporation, novation, clearing members, determination of obligations.
Day 9: Settlement Process — settlement cycles, pay-in and pay-out of funds and securities, shortages, auctions and close-out.
Day 10: First full-length timed mock test and a detailed review of every explanation.

sections.heading: Days 11–15: grievances, other services and mocks
paragraphs: The last stretch covers the remaining chapters and builds exam stamina.
bullets: Day 11: Investor Grievances and Arbitration — grievance redressal mechanisms, the online dispute resolution framework, arbitration process as described in the workbook.
Day 12: Other Services Provided by Brokers — depository services, margin trading facility, mutual fund and IPO distribution, and similar services; then a second mock.
Day 13: Revise risk management, clearing and settlement with your flowcharts; rework every error from the mocks.
Day 14: Third full-length mock and review.
Day 15: Light revision of summaries and error log only. Sleep early.

sections.heading: Revision method for an operations exam
paragraphs: Operations questions reward knowing sequences and responsibilities. For each process — account opening, order to trade, clearing, settlement, grievance redressal — write the steps in order and the entity responsible for each. Test yourself by covering one column and recalling the other.

Keep a separate sheet for numbers and timelines mentioned in the workbook, such as settlement cycles and deadlines. Exchanges and SEBI revise these periodically, so take them only from the current workbook edition on nism.ac.in, not from old notes or videos.
bullets: Draw the clearing and settlement flow at least three times from memory.
List each type of margin with what it covers and when it is collected.
Note who handles each kind of grievance and at what stage arbitration applies.

sections.heading: Using mock tests well
paragraphs: Three full-length timed mock tests are usually enough for Series VII if you review them properly. Sit each in a single 120-minute block, then go through the explanations for every wrong and guessed answer. Sort mistakes by chapter; if most come from risk management or settlement, return to your flowcharts rather than re-reading the whole chapter.

Also track your accuracy on attempted questions. With a 50 percent pass mark, a candidate who attempts 80 questions at 85 percent accuracy is far safer than one who attempts all 100 at 65 percent, because each wrong answer also costs a quarter mark. If your accuracy is low, the fix is usually more careful reading of process questions rather than more hours with the workbook.

sections.heading: Exam-day tips
paragraphs: Do one complete pass answering everything you are sure of and marking the rest. Most candidates finish this in about 70 minutes. Use the remaining time for marked questions, attempting only those where you can eliminate two options. Read process questions twice; a word like 'before', 'after' or 'not' often decides the answer.

faqs: Is 15 days enough for NISM Series VII?

For most candidates who can study around two hours a day, 15 days is enough, especially if you already work in broking operations. Complete beginners may want three weeks, giving more time to risk management, clearing and settlement, and to taking additional timed practice tests.
Which chapters are most important for NISM VII?

Based on the syllabus, Risk Management, Clearing Process and Settlement Process tend to carry the most weight, followed by broking operations, market participants and investor grievances. NISM does not publish an official split, so read every chapter and use weightage only to plan revision.
Are there calculations in NISM Series VII?

There are some, mainly on margins, mark-to-market and settlement obligations, but the exam is largely process-based. Most questions test whether you know the correct sequence of steps, the entity responsible and the rules described in the workbook.

guides.title: NISM Series VII Syllabus Explained Chapter by Chapter
guides.description: NISM Series VII syllabus explained chapter by chapter: what each Securities Operations and Risk Management topic covers and where to focus your study.
secondary: nism securities operations and risk management syllabus
guides.intro: The NISM Series VII syllabus covers what happens after an investor clicks 'buy': how a broker processes the order, how the trade is cleared, how money and securities move, how risk is controlled and how disputes are resolved. Securities Operations and Risk Management is designed for back-office, settlement and risk staff, so it tests processes and responsibilities more than theory. This guide explains each chapter, the kind of questions it produces and what to focus on, so you can read the official workbook from nism.ac.in with a clear map in mind.

sections.heading: The big picture
paragraphs: The syllabus moves in a logical order: first the market and its participants, then broking operations, then the risk, clearing and settlement chain, and finally grievance redressal and additional services. The indicative pattern is 100 questions for 100 marks in 120 minutes, with a 50 percent pass mark and 0.25 negative marking — indicative, so confirm in the latest official notification on nism.ac.in.

Because operational rules are revised by SEBI and the exchanges, NISM updates the workbook periodically. Always check the edition and effective date before you begin, and study timelines and limits only from that edition.

As you read, notice that chapters 4, 5 and 6 describe a single continuous chain: risk is managed before and during trading, obligations are determined in clearing, and they are discharged in settlement. Studying them together, rather than as three separate topics, makes the whole syllabus much easier to retain.

sections.heading: Chapters 1 and 2: the securities market and its participants
paragraphs: This chapter sets the scene: the role of securities markets in an economy, primary and secondary markets, the products traded — equity, debt, derivatives, mutual fund units — and the regulators and market infrastructure institutions. Questions are mostly definitional and quick to answer, making it a good chapter to secure early marks.
Focus on the distinction between primary and secondary markets, the functions of exchanges, clearing corporations and depositories, and the broad responsibilities of SEBI.

Here you meet everyone in the chain: investors, stock brokers, clearing members, custodians, depositories and depository participants, clearing banks, registrars and merchant bankers. Expect questions on who does what and who is regulated by whom.

A simple table with each participant, its role and its regulator is the most effective way to learn this chapter. Many wrong answers come from confusing clearing members with trading members, or custodians with depository participants.

sections.heading: Chapter 3: Introduction to Securities Broking Operations
paragraphs: This chapter covers the front-to-back workflow inside a broking firm: client registration and KYC, account opening documents, risk disclosure, order entry and management, trade confirmation and contract notes, and the back-office functions that support them. Questions are practical — for example, which document must be issued after a trade, or what a broker must verify before activating a client.
Learn the sequence of steps from client onboarding to trade confirmation, and the documents and records involved at each step.

Contract notes, client registration documents and the rights and obligations of brokers and clients are common question areas, so read those parts of the chapter slowly and note any specific timelines the workbook mentions.

sections.heading: Chapter 4: Risk Management
paragraphs: Risk management is one of the most important chapters. It explains how exchanges and clearing corporations protect the system from default: types of margins, margin collection and reporting, mark-to-market settlement, position limits, capital adequacy requirements and surveillance measures. Some questions involve simple calculations on margins or mark-to-market.

Focus on what each margin covers, who collects it from whom and when, and how risk containment measures respond when limits are breached. Draw the margin flow from client to broker to clearing member to clearing corporation.

sections.heading: Chapter 5: Clearing Process
paragraphs: This chapter explains how trades become obligations. It covers the role of the clearing corporation, novation (the clearing corporation becoming counterparty to every trade), clearing members and custodians, and how net obligations are determined for funds and securities.

Questions often test the concept of novation, the difference between gross and net obligations, and the responsibilities of clearing banks. A worked example of netting several trades for one member is the best way to master it.

It is worth working through at least one simple numerical by hand: a client's position over three days, the daily mark-to-market amount, and the effect on the margin balance. Once you have done this yourself, multiple-choice questions on the topic feel familiar rather than intimidating.

sections.heading: Chapter 6: Settlement Process
paragraphs: Settlement is where obligations are discharged: pay-in and pay-out of funds and securities, settlement cycles, handling of shortages, auctions and close-out, and corporate action adjustments. This chapter overlaps with risk management and clearing, and together the three form the core of the exam.

Learn the settlement cycle as described in the current workbook and the sequence of events within it. Pay attention to what happens when a seller fails to deliver, because shortage handling and auctions are a favourite question area.

sections.heading: Chapter 7: Investor Grievances and Arbitration
paragraphs: This chapter explains how investors raise complaints and how they are resolved: the broker's internal redressal, exchange mechanisms, SEBI's complaint systems and the online dispute resolution and arbitration framework as described in the workbook. Questions are factual and often test the order of escalation and timelines.
Since grievance frameworks have been updated in recent years, rely only on the current workbook and verify any details on the official SEBI and exchange websites.
Make sure you understand which complaints go first to the broker, when the exchange steps in and how the process moves to conciliation or arbitration, since sequence questions are common.

sections.heading: Chapter 8: Other Services Provided by Brokers
paragraphs: The final chapter covers services beyond plain trading: depository participant services, margin trading facility, securities lending and borrowing, distribution of mutual funds and IPOs, and similar offerings. Questions test the basic features and conditions of each service.

Based on the syllabus, chapters 4, 5 and 6 tend to carry the most weight, with chapters 2, 3 and 7 next. Read every chapter at least twice, practise chapter-wise questions after each one, and finish with full-length timed mock tests and a careful review of their explanations.

A sensible study order is to cover chapters 1 to 3 in the first few days, spend the longest stretch on chapters 4 to 6 with flowcharts and worked examples, and then finish chapters 7 and 8, which are shorter and factual. Keep a single page of timelines and limits from the workbook and revise it every day in the final week.

faqs: How many chapters are in the NISM Series VII syllabus?

The current syllabus is organised into about eight chapters, from an introduction to the securities market through risk management, clearing and settlement to investor grievances and other broker services. Download the latest workbook from nism.ac.in to confirm the chapter list for your exam date.
Which part of the NISM VII syllabus is most important?

Based on the syllabus, risk management, the clearing process and the settlement process form the core of the exam and tend to carry the most questions. Broking operations, market participants and investor grievances follow. Cover every chapter, as the remaining ones provide quick marks.
Is the NISM Series VII syllabus difficult?

It is not conceptually difficult, but it is detailed. Questions test exact processes, responsibilities and timelines, and negative marking punishes guesswork. Candidates who draw flowcharts for margins, clearing and settlement and practise chapter-wise questions usually find the syllabus manageable in two to three weeks.

guides.title: How to Prepare for NISM Series VI in 15 Days
guides.description: A 15-day NISM Series VI study plan for Depository Operations: daily chapter schedule, approximate weightage, revision method and timed mock tests.
guides.primary: how to prepare for nism series vi
secondary: how to pass nism series vi
guides.intro: Employees of depository participants often have to clear the Depository Operations certification within weeks of joining, so knowing how to prepare for NISM Series VI efficiently matters. The syllabus covers the depository system, NSDL and CDSL, account opening and operations, transmission and nomination, dematerialisation, trading and settlement, pledge, corporate actions, debt and government securities, foreign portfolio investors and investor services. It is detailed rather than difficult, and the pass mark is higher than some NISM papers. This guide gives a 15-day plan, approximate weightage, a revision routine and a mock-test schedule.

sections.heading: Exam pattern and why precision matters
paragraphs: The indicative pattern is 100 questions carrying 100 marks in 120 minutes, with a pass mark of 60 percent and negative marking of 0.25 marks per wrong answer. Treat these as indicative — confirm in the latest official notification on nism.ac.in before you register.

A 60 percent pass line with negative marking means you need roughly 65 correct answers with few mistakes. Most Series VI questions test specific procedures — which form is used, who signs, what happens when a holder dies, how a pledge is closed — so vague familiarity is not enough. The plan below is built around learning each procedure step by step.

sections.heading: Approximate chapter weightage
paragraphs: NISM does not publish an official chapter-wise split. Based on the syllabus and the length of each workbook chapter, this grouping is approximate.
bullets: High: DP Functions – Account Opening; DP Functions – Account Operations; DP Functions – Dematerialisation; DP Functions – Transmission and Nomination.

Medium: Introduction to Depository; Depository and its Business Partners; DP Functions – Trading and Settlement; Special Services – Pledge & Hypothecation; Special Services – Public Offering / Corporate Actions.
Lower but direct: Introduction to the Indian Capital Market; Special Services – Debt Instruments & Government Securities; Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPI); Investor Services.
Very few questions involve calculations; nearly all test procedures, roles and definitions.

sections.heading: Who should adjust the plan
paragraphs: Fifteen days assumes about two hours on weekdays and three hours at weekends. If you already work at a DP desk handling account opening and transfers, several chapters will be familiar and you could finish in ten days, spending the saved time on mock tests. If you are new to the securities industry, allow about three weeks and spend extra time on the account operations and transmission chapters, which carry many questions and involve several similar-looking procedures.

Use the current workbook from nism.ac.in as your only reference for procedures and timelines. Depository processes are updated through SEBI circulars and depository operating instructions, and questions follow the workbook edition.

sections.heading: Days 1–5: the depository system and account opening
paragraphs: Read each chapter, write a one-page summary and finish with chapter-wise practice questions.
bullets: Day 1: Introduction to the Indian Capital Market — primary and secondary markets, intermediaries, the shift from physical to electronic holding.
Day 2: Introduction to Depository — the depository concept, benefits of dematerialised holding, the legal framework, NSDL and CDSL.
Day 3: Depository and its Business Partners — DPs, issuers, RTAs, clearing corporations and their relationship with the depository.
Days 4–5: DP Functions – Account Opening — types of beneficial owner accounts, KYC, documents for individuals and non-individuals, joint holdings, account closure.

sections.heading: Days 6–10: core DP operations
paragraphs: These chapters contain the most questions. Draw a flow diagram for every process and note which form or instruction is involved at each step.
bullets: Day 6: DP Functions – Account Operations — delivery instructions, off-market and market transfers, freezing and unfreezing, change of details.
Day 7: DP Functions – Transmission and Nomination — nomination rules, transmission on death of a sole or joint holder, documents required.
Day 8: DP Functions – Dematerialisation — the demat request flow from client to DP to RTA to depository, rematerialisation, rejection reasons.
Day 9: DP Functions – Trading and Settlement — pay-in and pay-out through the depository, settlement-related instructions.
Day 10: First full-length timed mock test and a detailed review of every explanation.

sections.heading: Days 11–15: special services, revision and mocks
paragraphs: The final stretch covers the special services chapters and builds exam rhythm.
bullets: Day 11: Special Services – Pledge & Hypothecation; Special Services – Public Offering / Corporate Actions.
Day 12: Special Services – Debt Instruments & Government Securities; Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPI); Investor Services. Second mock in the evening.
Day 13: Revise account operations, transmission and dematerialisation using your flow diagrams; rework every mock error.
Day 14: Third full-length mock and review.
Day 15: Light revision of summaries and error log only; check your test centre details.

sections.heading: A revision method built for procedures
paragraphs: For every process, write three things: the trigger (what the client wants), the steps in order with the entity responsible, and the outcome. Then test yourself by covering the steps and reconstructing them. This works far better than re-reading, because exam questions often present the steps out of order or swap the responsible entity.

Keep a comparison table for pairs that are easy to confuse: nomination versus transmission, pledge versus hypothecation, freezing versus closing an account, market versus off-market transfer, dematerialisation versus rematerialisation. A large share of wrong answers in this exam comes from mixing up such pairs.
bullets: Revise flow diagrams daily from Day 6 onwards.
Keep a short sheet of timelines and limits from the workbook.
Maintain an error log and read it every evening in the final week.

sections.heading: Common mistakes to avoid
paragraphs: The most frequent mistake in Series VI is treating NSDL and CDSL terminology as interchangeable without checking how the workbook describes each process. Another is studying from summaries or older notes; depository procedures, forms and timelines are revised through SEBI circulars, and outdated details produce confidently wrong answers. A third is skipping the shorter chapters on FPIs, government securities and investor services because they look peripheral. They are quick to learn and supply direct, factual questions that help you clear the 60 percent line without stress.

sections.heading: Mock tests and exam-day approach
paragraphs: Three full-length timed mock tests in the final week are usually enough. Sit each one in a single 120-minute block and then review the explanations for every wrong and guessed answer; that review is where most improvement happens. Track accuracy on attempted questions and aim to keep it above 80 percent.

On exam day, answer every question you are sure of in a first pass of about 70 minutes, marking the rest. Return to marked questions and attempt only those where you can eliminate at least two options. Read procedural questions twice; words like 'not', 'first' and 'only' frequently decide the answer.

faqs: Is 15 days enough to prepare for NISM Series VI?

For most candidates who can study around two hours a day, especially those already working at a depository participant, 15 days is enough. Freshers to the securities industry should allow about three weeks, giving extra time to account operations, transmission and dematerialisation procedures.
Which chapters are most important in NISM VI?

Based on the syllabus, the DP functions chapters — account opening, account operations, transmission and nomination, and dematerialisation — tend to carry the most questions. Pledge, corporate actions and trading and settlement follow. NISM does not publish an official split, so read every chapter.
What is the pass mark for NISM Series VI?

The indicative pattern has a pass mark of 60 percent, with 100 questions in 120 minutes and 0.25 negative marking per wrong answer. Patterns can change, so confirm the current details in the latest official notification on nism.ac.in before booking your exam.

guides.title: NISM Series VI Toughest Chapters and How to Score
guides.description: The toughest NISM Series VI chapters — account operations, transmission, demat, pledge and corporate actions — with practical ways to score in each one.
secondary: nism series vi transmission and nomination
how to score in nism series vi
guides.intro: Depository Operations is not a mathematical exam, yet many candidates are surprised by how hard some chapters feel. The NISM Series VI toughest chapters share one feature: they describe procedures with several similar steps, forms and exceptions, and the questions test those details precisely. With an indicative pass mark of 60 percent and negative marking, weak spots in these chapters can decide the result. This guide identifies the chapters candidates struggle with most, explains why, and gives practical techniques to turn each into a scoring area.

sections.heading: Why procedural chapters feel hard
paragraphs: The indicative pattern is 100 questions for 100 marks in 120 minutes, with a 60 percent pass mark and 0.25 negative marking — indicative, so confirm in the latest official notification on nism.ac.in. Time is rarely the problem; precision is.

Procedural chapters are hard because the options in a question are usually all plausible steps from real processes. Only one matches the exact situation described — the right form, the right sequence, the right entity. Reading the chapter once creates a general picture but not the detail needed to pick between near-identical options.

There is also a vocabulary challenge. Terms such as beneficial owner, delivery instruction, freeze, transmission and invocation have precise meanings in the depository context, and questions often use them without explanation. Keeping a short glossary while you study saves time later.

sections.heading: 1. DP Functions – Transmission and Nomination
paragraphs: This is the chapter candidates most often name as the hardest. It covers nomination rules for individual and joint accounts, how nomination is made, changed or cancelled, and transmission of securities after the death of a sole holder, one joint holder or all joint holders. Each situation needs different documents and follows a different route, and questions describe the situation briefly and ask what happens next.

How to score: build a grid with situations as rows — sole holder with nominee, sole holder without nominee, death of one joint holder, death of all joint holders — and columns for who can claim, documents required, and where the securities go. Learn the grid until you can reproduce it. Then practise situation-based questions until you can identify the row within seconds.

sections.heading: 2. DP Functions – Account Operations
paragraphs: Account operations covers the day-to-day life of a demat account: delivery instruction slips, market and off-market transfers, inter-depository transfers, freezing and unfreezing, change of address, bank details or signatures, and account closure. The volume of rules is large, and many questions turn on small conditions — for example, who must sign an instruction for a joint account.

How to score: group the operations into three families — transfers, account changes, and freeze or closure — and for each family list the instruction used, the signatories and the checks the DP must perform. Practise chapter-wise questions immediately after studying each family, rather than reading the whole chapter first.
bullets: Know the difference between market and off-market transfers and when each is used.
Note who must sign instructions for joint accounts.
Learn the conditions under which an account can be closed and what happens to remaining balances.

sections.heading: 3. DP Functions – Dematerialisation
paragraphs: Dematerialisation involves several parties — the client, the DP, the RTA or issuer, and the depository — and both physical documents and electronic requests. Questions test the order of steps, who verifies what, the reasons a request may be rejected and how rematerialisation differs.

How to score: draw the demat flow as a diagram with arrows between client, DP, RTA and depository, labelling what moves along each arrow — certificates, the request form or electronic confirmation. Draw it from memory three times on separate days. Then do the same for rematerialisation and compare the two diagrams.

sections.heading: 4. Special Services – Pledge & Hypothecation
paragraphs: Pledge questions are tricky because pledge and hypothecation look similar and the process involves both the pledgor's and pledgee's DPs. Questions ask about creation, closure and invocation of a pledge, and the difference in rights between pledge and hypothecation as described in the workbook.

How to score: write the pledge life cycle in four lines — initiation by pledgor, acceptance by pledgee, closure on repayment, invocation on default — with the party acting at each stage. Then add one line on how hypothecation differs. This compact summary handles most questions on the topic.

sections.heading: 5. Special Services – Public Offering / Corporate Actions
paragraphs: This chapter covers credit of securities after an IPO and the handling of corporate actions such as bonus issues, rights issues, splits, mergers and dividends in a depository environment. Questions test who initiates a corporate action, how record dates work and how the depository credits or debits accounts.

How to score: make a table with each corporate action, what changes in the client's holding, and the role of the issuer, RTA and depository. Most questions become straightforward once you see that the issuer or RTA initiates and the depository executes.

sections.heading: Easier chapters you should still secure
paragraphs: Spending most of your time on the tough chapters is sensible, but do not neglect the shorter ones. They are largely definitional and offer good marks per hour of study.
bullets: Introduction to the Indian Capital Market and Introduction to Depository — concepts, benefits and the legal framework.
Depository and its Business Partners — roles of DPs, issuers, RTAs and clearing corporations.
DP Functions – Account Opening — account types, KYC and documents.
Special Services – Debt Instruments & Government Securities, Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPI) and Investor Services — features and rules as described in the workbook.

sections.heading: Putting it together in practice
paragraphs: Allocate roughly 60 percent of your preparation time to the five chapters above and 40 percent to the rest. After every chapter, attempt chapter-wise practice questions; in the final week, take full-length timed mock tests and spend as long reviewing the explanations as you spent on the test. Sort mistakes by chapter, and if transmission or account operations still dominate the list, return to your grids and diagrams rather than re-reading.

On exam day, read each procedural question twice and identify the exact situation — sole or joint, living or deceased, pledgor or pledgee — before looking at the options. With negative marking, attempt a doubtful question only after eliminating at least two options.

Finally, remember that the workbook is the reference for every answer. Depository procedures are updated through SEBI circulars and depository operating instructions, so study from the current edition on nism.ac.in and treat older notes, videos or forum posts with caution, particularly for timelines and document lists.

faqs: Which is the hardest chapter in NISM Series VI?

Many candidates find Transmission and Nomination the hardest, followed by Account Operations and Dematerialisation. These chapters involve several similar procedures, forms and exceptions, and questions test exact details. Building comparison grids and flow diagrams is the most effective way to master them.
How should I study pledge and hypothecation for NISM VI?

Write the pledge life cycle as four stages — initiation, acceptance, closure and invocation — with the party acting at each step. Then note how hypothecation differs in rights and process. Practise situation-based questions until you can identify the stage quickly.
Are there numerical questions in NISM Series VI?

Very few, if any. The exam is almost entirely procedural and conceptual, testing the steps, forms, responsibilities and rules of depository operations. Precision in reading the question and knowing exact procedures matters far more than calculation skills.

guides.title: How to Prepare for NISM Series XXI-A in 21 Days
guides.description: A 21-day NISM Series XXI-A study plan for PMS Distributors: weekly chapters, approximate weightage, return calculations, revision and timed mock tests.
guides.primary: how to prepare for nism series xxi-a
secondary: how to pass nism series xxi-a
guides.intro: Relationship managers who distribute Portfolio Management Services usually need this certification, and the most common question is how to prepare for NISM Series XXI-A alongside a full-time job. The syllabus starts with investment basics across equity, fixed income and derivatives, then moves to collective investment vehicles, the role and operations of portfolio managers, the portfolio management process, performance measurement, taxation and SEBI's PMS regulations. A 21-day plan gives enough time for the calculation chapters and several full-length tests. This guide lays out the schedule week by week, with approximate weightage and a revision routine.

sections.heading: Exam pattern and preparation approach
paragraphs: The indicative pattern is 100 questions carrying 100 marks in 120 minutes, with a pass mark of 60 percent and negative marking of 0.25 marks per wrong answer. Treat these as indicative — confirm in the latest official notification on nism.ac.in.

The 60 percent pass line is the key number. It means you need around 65 correct answers with few mistakes, so you cannot rely on the regulatory chapter alone. Candidates with a mutual fund background often find the investment chapters comfortable but are caught out by PMS-specific operational and regulatory details, and by performance measurement questions.

sections.heading: Who should adjust the timeline
paragraphs: Twenty-one days assumes about two hours on weekdays and three hours at weekends. If you have recently cleared NISM V-A or X-A, the investment foundation chapters will feel familiar; you can compress Week 1 into four days and use the saved time for an extra mock test or deeper work on PMS operations. If equity valuation and bond maths are new to you, extend Week 1 to ten days, because later chapters on the portfolio process and performance measurement assume this foundation.

Also check the latest workbook on nism.ac.in before you start. SEBI has revised PMS regulations, disclosure requirements and performance reporting norms several times in recent years, and NISM updates the workbook to reflect them. Studying from an outdated edition is a common and avoidable cause of lost marks, especially in the regulatory chapter.
It is worth asking your employer or compliance team whether they have a preferred exam window, since many firms schedule certification deadlines around onboarding or annual renewal cycles.

sections.heading: Approximate chapter weightage
paragraphs: NISM does not publish an official chapter-wise split. Based on the syllabus and the depth of workbook chapters, the following grouping is approximate.
bullets: High: Role of Portfolio Managers; Operational Aspects of Portfolio Managers; Portfolio Management Process; Regulatory, Governance and Ethical Aspects of Portfolio Managers.
Medium: Investing in Stocks; Investing in Fixed Income Securities; Performance Measurement and Evaluation of Portfolio Managers; Collective Investment Vehicles.
Lower but direct: Investments; Introduction to Securities Markets; Derivatives; Taxation.
Calculation areas: returns (absolute, annualised, time-weighted concepts as covered in the workbook), risk measures, risk-adjusted ratios and basic bond and equity valuation.

sections.heading: Week 1: investment foundations
paragraphs: Study about two hours on weekdays and three hours at weekends. End each day with chapter-wise practice questions while the material is fresh.
bullets: Day 1: Investments — the concept of investment, risk and return, asset classes.
Day 2: Introduction to Securities Markets — primary and secondary markets, participants and regulators.
Days 3–4: Investing in Stocks — equity research basics, valuation ratios, approaches to stock selection.
Days 5–6: Investing in Fixed Income Securities — bond features, yields, price-yield relationship, credit risk and duration at the level covered in the workbook.
Day 7: Derivatives — futures and options basics and their use in portfolios; revision of Week 1.

sections.heading: Week 2: PMS in depth
paragraphs: This is the most important week. Focus on how a PMS differs from other managed products and how it is run day to day.
bullets: Day 8: Collective Investment Vehicles — mutual funds, AIFs and other pooled products, and how PMS compares.
Days 9–10: Role of Portfolio Managers — discretionary, non-discretionary and advisory services; the portfolio manager's responsibilities; client agreements and disclosure documents.
Days 11–12: Operational Aspects of Portfolio Managers — client onboarding, account structure, custody, fees and their computation methods as described in the workbook, reporting to clients.
Days 13–14: Portfolio Management Process — investment policy, asset allocation, strategy, rebalancing; then a first full-length timed mock test with review.

sections.heading: Week 3: performance, tax, regulation and mocks
paragraphs: The final week covers the remaining technical and regulatory chapters and builds exam stamina.
bullets: Days 15–16: Performance Measurement and Evaluation of Portfolio Managers — return calculations, benchmarks, risk-adjusted measures such as Sharpe and Treynor, and the performance reporting norms described in the workbook.
Day 17: Taxation — tax treatment of PMS investments as described in the current workbook edition.
Day 18: Regulatory, Governance and Ethical Aspects of Portfolio Managers — SEBI PMS regulations, distributor obligations, code of conduct. Read twice.
Day 19: Second full-length mock and detailed review.
Day 20: Rework every error; third mock in the evening.
Day 21: Light revision of formula sheet, regulatory notes and error log.

sections.heading: Revision techniques for XXI-A
paragraphs: Create a comparison table of PMS, mutual funds and AIFs with rows for structure, minimum investment as stated in the workbook, ownership of securities, customisation, fees, transparency and taxation. Many questions ask how PMS differs from a fund, and one table answers most of them. Take any thresholds or limits only from the current workbook, because SEBI revises them.

For performance measurement, keep a formula sheet and re-solve every problem you got wrong in practice. For regulation, write each key obligation as a short question-and-answer card and revise the cards on at least four separate days.
bullets: Maintain an error log with chapter, concept and correction.
Revise the PMS vs mutual fund vs AIF table daily in Week 3.
Practise fee computation examples from the workbook by hand.

sections.heading: Mock tests and exam-day approach
paragraphs: Take three full-length timed mock tests in the final week, each in a single 120-minute sitting, and review the explanation for every wrong or guessed answer. Track accuracy on attempted questions; with a 60 percent pass mark and negative marking, aim to keep it above 80 percent.

On exam day, answer everything you are sure of in a first pass, marking calculation and long scenario questions. Use the remaining time for marked questions and guess only where you have eliminated at least two options. Keep ten minutes at the end to check for unanswered questions you meant to attempt.

After the exam, keep your comparison table and regulatory notes. They double as a handy reference when explaining PMS features, costs and risks to clients, which is the everyday work the certification is designed to support.

faqs: Is 21 days enough to prepare for NISM Series XXI-A?

For most working professionals who can study two to three hours a day, 21 days is a realistic window. Those who have already cleared NISM V-A or work in wealth management may need around two weeks. Complete beginners should allow four weeks, with extra time on fixed income and performance measurement.
Which chapters are most important for NISM XXI-A?

Based on the syllabus, the chapters on the role of portfolio managers, operational aspects, the portfolio management process and regulation tend to carry the most weight. Investment basics, performance measurement and collective investment vehicles follow. NISM does not publish an official split.
Does NISM XXI-A have calculation questions?

Yes, though they are not the majority. Expect some questions on returns, risk measures, risk-adjusted ratios, bond yields and possibly fee computation. The arithmetic is simple, but practising the formulas from the workbook makes these questions quick and reliable.

guides.title: NISM XXI-A vs XXI-B: Which PMS Certification Do You Need?
guides.description: NISM XXI-A vs XXI-B explained: who needs the PMS Distributors exam, who needs Portfolio Managers, and how syllabus, pattern and preparation differ.
secondary: difference between nism xxi-a and xxi-b
nism pms distributors vs portfolio managers
guides.intro: Two NISM certifications relate to Portfolio Management Services, and the NISM XXI-A vs XXI-B question confuses many candidates. Both cover PMS, both carry negative marking and both have a 60 percent pass mark in their indicative patterns, yet they are meant for different roles. Series XXI-A is for distributors who sell PMS products to clients. Series XXI-B is for people working inside a portfolio management firm, typically in investment decision-making or key managerial roles. This guide explains who needs which, how the syllabus and pattern differ, and how to prepare.

sections.heading: The short answer
paragraphs: If you are a relationship manager, wealth manager or distributor who introduces clients to PMS products offered by portfolio managers, XXI-A is the relevant certification. If you work for a portfolio manager — particularly as the principal officer or in a role involved in investment decisions — XXI-B is the relevant one.

The precise categories of persons who must hold each certificate are set by SEBI regulations and circulars, which are revised from time to time. Confirm the current requirement on sebi.gov.in and check the exam details on nism.ac.in before you register.

sections.heading: Pattern comparison
paragraphs: The indicative patterns below are based on the current exam structure as we understand it. Treat them as indicative — confirm in the latest official notification on nism.ac.in.
bullets: XXI-A (PMS Distributors): 100 questions, 100 marks, 120 minutes, pass mark 60 percent, 0.25 negative marking per wrong answer.
XXI-B (Portfolio Managers): 100 questions, 100 marks, 180 minutes, pass mark 60 percent, 0.25 negative marking per wrong answer.
The extra hour in XXI-B reflects deeper, more analytical questions, including more on portfolio construction, analysis and risk.
Both papers require similar exam discipline because of the same pass mark and negative marking.

sections.heading: What XXI-A focuses on
paragraphs: XXI-A is built around what a distributor needs to explain PMS correctly and sell it responsibly. It covers investment basics across equity, fixed income and derivatives, how PMS compares with mutual funds and other collective investment vehicles, the role and operations of portfolio managers, the portfolio management process at a conceptual level, performance measurement and reporting, taxation, and the regulatory, governance and ethical obligations relevant to distribution.
The emphasis is on understanding products, communicating risks and costs clearly, matching PMS to suitable clients and following the conduct rules that apply to distributors.

sections.heading: What XXI-B focuses on
paragraphs: XXI-B goes further into how a portfolio manager actually runs money. Beyond the shared foundations, it typically covers equity and fixed income analysis in more depth, portfolio construction and risk management, the investment decision process, operational and compliance responsibilities of the portfolio manager, performance measurement and attribution, and the regulatory framework from the manager's side.

Questions are more analytical. Where XXI-A might ask what a risk-adjusted ratio indicates, XXI-B is more likely to expect you to apply it or compare portfolios using it. Check the current XXI-B workbook on nism.ac.in for its exact chapter list, as NISM revises workbooks periodically.

Because XXI-A candidates often come from mutual fund distribution, it is worth noting what feels new: the ownership of securities directly in the client's name, the customised nature of portfolios, fee structures that may include performance-linked components, and the specific disclosure and reporting obligations that apply to PMS. These are the areas where questions tend to separate prepared candidates from those relying on mutual fund knowledge alone.

sections.heading: Key differences at a glance
paragraphs: Seen side by side, the two certifications differ in purpose and depth more than in topic names.

Put simply, XXI-A asks whether you can explain and recommend a PMS responsibly, while XXI-B asks whether you can run one responsibly. Keeping that distinction in mind makes it easier to read each workbook with the right emphasis.
bullets: Audience: XXI-A for distributors of PMS; XXI-B for persons in the portfolio manager's organisation, especially in investment and key managerial roles.
Perspective: XXI-A explains PMS from the client-facing side; XXI-B from the investment and operational side.
Depth: XXI-B goes deeper into analysis, portfolio construction and risk.
Duration: 120 minutes for XXI-A versus 180 minutes for XXI-B in the indicative patterns.
Preparation time: typically two to three weeks for XXI-A and four to six weeks for XXI-B.

sections.heading: Can one certificate substitute for the other?
paragraphs: Generally, no. Each certificate is linked to specific roles by SEBI's requirements, so you should take the one that matches your role. Some professionals move between roles over their careers — a distributor who later joins a portfolio management firm, for example — and may eventually need both.

If you expect such a move, preparing for XXI-A first builds a useful foundation. Most of its investment and PMS concepts reappear in XXI-B, where they are extended with deeper analysis and the manager's responsibilities.

sections.heading: Questions to ask before you register
paragraphs: If you are still unsure which certificate applies to you, a few practical questions usually settle it. Discuss them with your compliance team, who will know how your firm interprets the current regulatory requirements.
bullets: Is your employer a SEBI-registered portfolio manager, or a distributor that offers PMS products from several portfolio managers?
Does your role involve selecting securities, constructing portfolios or approving investment decisions, or does it involve explaining and recommending PMS to clients?
Are you, or will you be, designated as a principal officer or in another key managerial position?
Does your appointment letter, onboarding checklist or compliance manual name a specific NISM series?
Are you planning a move from distribution to portfolio management, or the reverse, in the next few years?

sections.heading: How to prepare for each
paragraphs: For XXI-A, a two-to-three-week plan works for most working professionals. Prioritise the role of portfolio managers, operational aspects, the portfolio management process and regulation, and build a comparison table of PMS, mutual funds and AIFs. Practise return and risk-adjusted ratio calculations until they are quick.

For XXI-B, plan four to six weeks. Spend more time on equity and fixed income analysis, portfolio construction, risk measures and performance evaluation, and read the regulatory chapters from the portfolio manager's perspective.

For both, finish with several full-length timed mock tests and review the explanations carefully. Because both exams deduct a quarter mark per wrong answer, track your accuracy on attempted questions and skip questions where you cannot eliminate at least two options.
If you have cleared XXI-A and later move to a portfolio manager, revisit your XXI-A notes before starting XXI-B; the overlap will save you a week or more.
bullets: Download the current workbook for your exam from nism.ac.in.
Practise chapter-wise questions after every chapter.
Keep a formula sheet and a regulatory notes sheet, revised daily in the final week.

faqs: Is NISM XXI-B harder than XXI-A?

Generally yes. XXI-B is meant for professionals involved in managing portfolios, so it goes deeper into analysis, portfolio construction and risk, and the indicative pattern allows 180 minutes against 120 for XXI-A. Both have a 60 percent pass mark and negative marking in their indicative patterns.
I distribute PMS products. Do I need XXI-B?

Distributors of PMS products are generally covered by Series XXI-A. XXI-B is aimed at persons working within a portfolio management firm, particularly in investment decision-making or key managerial roles. Confirm the latest requirements on sebi.gov.in and nism.ac.in, as they can change.
Does XXI-A preparation help with XXI-B?

Yes. The investment basics, PMS concepts, performance measurement and regulatory framework from XXI-A form a solid base for XXI-B. You will still need to add deeper equity and fixed income analysis, portfolio construction, risk management and the portfolio manager's operational and compliance responsibilities.
